1498.text: In 2Thess.2.13 'we ought always to give thanks to God for you' diverges from the meal-blessing sense dominant in the Gospels/Acts/1Cor occurrences of this cluster -- here thanksgiving is a sustained, obligatory disposition ('ought always') directed at other believers' salvation-status (election, sanctification, belief) rather than a single ritual act over food. The impact is to broaden eucharisteo from a punctual liturgical gesture to an ongoing pastoral duty of gratitude for others' spiritual condition.

1503.text: In 2Thess.2.13, thanksgiving (G2168) co-occurs with M14 (brothers), M51 (beloved), M64 (chose), M16 (firstfruits), M79 (saved), M61 (sanctification), M13 (belief/truth, twice). Thanksgiving is the responsive frame surrounding this entire chain: it is offered specifically because of God's prior acts of choosing, sanctifying, and saving -- thanksgiving here functions as the grateful acknowledgment of the whole soteriological sequence rather than being caused by any single other M-code term alone.

This is the dominant register of the strong internally and forms the baseline against which the meal-blessing and single exceptional uses (below) stand out.

12481.text: God chooses a person for a task or office: priests and Levites, the king, David, Solomon, the servant, witnesses. The choice is shown, not argued: "the staff of the man whom I choose shall sprout" (Num 17:5). It is followed by a charge: "the Lord has chosen you to build a house for the sanctuary; be strong and do it" (1Ch 28:10). In the servant it is joined to God's soul and Spirit: "my chosen, in whom my soul delights; I have put my Spirit upon him" (Isa 42:1; Mat 12:18).

12482.text: God chooses a people, and the verses give love as the ground and deny number: "It was not because you were more in number than any other people that the Lord set his love on you and chose you" (Deu 7:7); "the Lord set his heart in love on your fathers and chose their offspring" (Deu 10:15). The choosing makes them "a people for his treasured possession" (Deu 7:6) and "his chosen ones" (Psa 105:6). It is joined to not casting off, "I have chosen you and not cast you off" (Isa 41:9), and to a purpose: "that you may know and believe me" (Isa 43:10).

12483.text: God chooses a place "to make his name dwell there" (Deu 12:11), and the choosing carries his own presence: "My eyes and my heart will be there for all time" (2Ch 7:16). The choice can be cast off, "I will cast off this city that I have chosen" (2Ki 23:27), and made again: "the Lord will again comfort Zion and again choose Jerusalem" (Zec 1:17).

12484.text: A person chooses the Lord, his ways and the good: "choose this day whom you will serve" (Jos 24:15), and the choice is witnessed: "You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen the Lord" (Jos 24:22); "I have chosen the way of faithfulness; I set your rules before me" (Psa 119:30); "who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant" (Isa 56:4). 12490.text: "Choice" as worth preferred over another: "To get understanding is to be chosen rather than silver" (Pro 16:16); "A good name is to be chosen rather than great riches" (Pro 22:1); "The tongue of the righteous is choice silver; the heart of the wicked is of little worth" (Pro 10:20); also Pro 8:10, 8:19 and Song 5:15.

12492.text: God chooses what he wants: "Is not this the fast that I choose: to loose the bonds of wickedness" (Isa 58:6), set against a fast of bowing the head (Isa 58:5); "To do righteousness and justice is more acceptable to the Lord than sacrifice" (Pro 21:3); "I will appoint over her whomever I choose. For who is like me?" (Jer 49:19; Jer 50:44).

12493.text: A person chooses against God: other gods, "the gods whom you have chosen; let them save you" (Judg 10:14); their own ways, "These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations" (Isa 66:3); what God does not delight in (Isa 65:12). The verses name what drives or follows such choosing: "your iniquity teaches your mouth, and you choose the tongue of the crafty" (Job 15:5); "Do not envy a man of violence and do not choose any of his ways" (Pro 3:31); "this you have chosen rather than affliction" (Job 36:21). Shame follows: "you shall blush for the gardens that you have chosen" (Isa 1:29); "an abomination is he who chooses you" (Isa 41:24).

12516.text: The will word is used of God, the Son and the Spirit: "anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him" (Mat 11:27; Luk 10:22); "Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done" (Luk 22:42); "For who can resist his will?" (Rom 9:19); the Spirit "who apportions to each one individually as he wills" (1Co 12:11); "Of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth" (Jam 1:18); "not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance" (2Pe 3:9).

12518.text: Looking ahead weighs before it acts: a king "will not sit down first and deliberate whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand" (Luk 14:31); "She considers a field and buys it" (Pro 31:16); "consider it, take counsel, and speak" (Judg 19:30). It plans without knowing: "on the chance that somehow they could reach Phoenix" (Act 27:12), "supposing that they had obtained their purpose" (Act 27:13), "they planned if possible to run the ship ashore" (Act 27:39). A plan carries a word: "Do I make my plans according to the flesh, ready to say Yes, yes and No, no at the same time?" (2Co 1:17). Plans part people: "Barnabas wanted to take with them John called Mark" (Act 15:37); Joseph of Arimathea "had not consented to their decision and action" (Luk 23:51). And a plan can be for another's good: "because an excellent spirit was in him. And the king planned to set him over the whole kingdom" (Dan 6:3).

14181.text: Part 2 verses: what they add: Kin offence hardens. "A brother offended is more unyielding than a strong city, and quarreling is like the bars of a castle" (Pro 18:19). The closer the tie, the harder the wall. This is the reverse of Gen 13's reason for yielding ("for we are kinsmen"); Brothers' anger takes the form of imposed labour: "My mother's sons were angry with me; they made me keeper of the vineyards, but my own vineyard I have not kept!" (Song 1:6). The anger is felt by the one it lands on as the loss of her own vineyard. The next verse turns straight to "you whom my soul loves" (1:7); Edom against his brother: anger that never turns away. Edom "pursued his brother with the sword and cast off all pity, and his anger tore perpetually, and he kept his wrath forever" (Amo 1:11). God will deal with Edom "according to the anger and envy that you showed because of your hatred against them" (Eze 35:11), with its speech: "They are given us to devour" (35:12); This is exactly the opposite of Gen 27:44–45. There Rebekah waits for Esau's anger to "turn away" and for him to "forget", and it does (Gen 33:4). Esau the man let his anger pass. Edom, his nation, "kept his wrath forever". The same bloodline shows anger's two courses; Amo 1:9 names the same failure for Tyre: "did not remember the covenant of brotherhood"; Anger at a brother judged like murder, and the remedy is reconciliation before worship: "everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment" (Mat 5:22); "leave your gift there before the altar and go. First be reconciled to your brother" (5:24). The worship waits on the relationship; Brothers in the work part without the yielding: "there arose a sharp disagreement, so that they separated from each other. Barnabas took Mark … but Paul chose Silas" (Act 15:39–40). It began over Mark, "who had withdrawn from them" (15:38). Separation, as in Gen 13:11, but here neither party gives the other the choice. Both are "commended … to the grace of the Lord" (15:40) and the work goes on in two directions; Seat : none in-verse or ±2. The next verse after Song 1:6 has "you whom my soul loves" (Song 1:7). Genuine. The bearer's own. The one who bears her brothers' anger turns at once to the one her soul loves.

14206.text: What it does. To this day I keep showing steadfast love to the house of Saul … And yet you charge me today with a fault concerning a woman" (2Sa 3:8); Elihu burns with anger three times (Job 32:2, 3, 5). (18:8); It attacks one's own son as the rival's ally: "You son of a perverse, rebellious woman … as long as the son of Jesse lives … neither you nor your kingdom shall be established" (20:30–31); It jeers: Sanballat "was angry and greatly enraged, and he jeered at the Jews … 'What are these feeble Jews doing?'" (Neh 4:1–2); It enlarges its target: Haman "disdained to lay hands on Mordecai alone … sought to destroy all the Jews" (Est 3:6).

15109.text: What the batch 1 verses state: The same words are used of God and of people. gāʾôn, gaʾăwāh, gēʾût and gāʾāh name God's majesty (Exo 15:1, 7; Psa 93:1; Isa 2:10) and human pride (Isa 9:9; Jer 48:29; Pro 16:18). So yes: these words describe a characteristic of God. In ESV English the difference shows in the choice of word ("majesty" against "pride"), not in the Hebrew; God's majesty is his own and is not taken on. He is "robed in majesty" while "you are from everlasting" (Psa 93:1–2). Nothing in these verses shows it being acquired. It is shown in acts: the sea, the overthrow, the thunder; It is challenged, but it is not overturned. The researcher's word "undisputed" needs one qualification from the verses. God's majesty is disputed: by the enemy at the sea (Exo 15:9), by "all that is proud and lofty" (Isa 2:12), and by the one who says "I will ascend to heaven" (Isa 14:13). Each time the dispute ends with the one who rose brought down. So it is not uncontested; it is never overturned; Majesty goes with what only God can do. Job 40:10–14 makes the test plain: whoever wears majesty must abase every proud one and save by his own hand. Only God does; Human pride in these verses is mostly a standing that is taken, or kept against God; It is said in the heart against the facts: "the bricks have fallen, but we will build" (Isa 9:10); It is worn as a show (Psa 73:6); It is set over the weak (Psa 10:2; Eze 16:49; Pro 15:25); It refuses to hear (Jer 13:15–17); It stands on might and strongholds (Lev 26:19; Amo 6:8; Eze 33:26); This agrees with the researcher's "mostly assumed"; But the same word for people is not always assumed. God gives a "pride" to his people: chosen (Psa 47:4), given (Isa 4:2), made (Isa 60:15), restored (Nah 2:2). The Lord himself is their "triumph" (Deu 33:29). The verses also show a given honour turned into pride (Eze 7:20; 24:21); I read: the line the verses draw is not between God having majesty and people having none. It runs between a standing that is one's own by nature (God), a standing given by God (his people), and a standing taken, or turned against the giver (pride); The Son's majesty is described as received, and it stands beside his being handed over; "he received honor and glory from God the Father" (2Pe 1:17); "after making purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty" (Heb 1:3); At the very moment of "the majesty of God", he speaks of being "delivered into the hands of men" (Luk 9:43–44); This joins 13.1 Lowering himself (M09): the one with majesty did not hold onto it in the way pride holds; I read: where Php 2:6–9 joins the two, it lies outside this batch's words; A majesty that depends on people is the contrast. Artemis's "magnificence" can be "deposed", because it rests on "she whom all Asia and the world worship" (Act 19:27). I read: this is the borrowed standing that pride is, set against God's majesty, which no one confers.

15188.text: Nothing to boast of before God: God chose "what is low and despised in the world ... so that no human being might boast in the presence of God" (1Co 1:28–29); "For by grace you have been saved through faith. It is excluded ... by the law of faith" (Rom 3:27); "if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not before God" (Rom 4:2); The ground of the exclusion is stated each time: a gift, a choosing of the low, faith.

15260.text: Refinement 2: the same words for people are not always pride: God gives a "pride" or majesty to his people: chosen (Psa 47:4), given (Isa 4:2), made (Isa 60:15), restored (Nah 2:2); A heart can be "courageous [lifted up] in the ways of the Lord" (2Ch 17:6); The boast can be moved to God (1Co 1:31; Rom 5:2–3, 11); The measure assigned by God is the right measure (Rom 12:3; 2Co 10:13); I read: the verses draw the line by source and direction, not by the word. I have calmed and quieted my soul" (Psa 131:1–2), set against the arrogant man "never at rest" (Hab 2:5).

15332.text: It always faces someone: "before me" (1Ki 21:29); "before the Lord" (2Ki 22:19); "before the God of his fathers" (2Ch 33:12); "before your God" (Dan 10:12); Zedekiah's failure is put as "He did not humble himself before Jeremiah the prophet, who spoke from the mouth of the Lord" (2Ch 36:12). Humbling before the prophet is humbling before the word he carries; Most verses in this group name before whom. Of the rest, 2Ch 12:6 and 2Ch 30:11 answer a word just brought, and Lev 26:41 goes with confession (26:40). Isa 58:3–5 is a fast addressed to God.

15344.text: A humbling God does not take knowledge of: Isa 58:3–5: The people ask: "Why have we fasted, and you see it not? Why have we humbled ourselves, and you take no knowledge of it?"; The answer: "in the day of your fast you seek your own pleasure, and oppress all your workers", and "you fast only to quarrel and to fight"; The form is named and set aside: "Is it to bow down his head like a reed, and to spread sackcloth and ashes under him?"; The fast God chooses is turned to others: "to loose the bonds of wickedness … to share your bread with the hungry and bring the homeless poor into your house; when you see the naked, to cover him" (58:6–7); Compare Ahab. His sackcloth and fasting were seen and answered (1Ki 21:27–29); I read: the outward acts are the same. What differs, by the two passages, is what goes with them. Ahab acts "when Ahab heard those words", against himself. In Isa 58 the fast is kept alongside self-pleasure and oppression. The humbling that is not taken knowledge of is one that leaves the seen poor unseen (58:7). This joins OT-105; 10.1, 10.7 and 13.1 already cite Isa 58:3, 5. The reading here is for the humbling side.

15429.text: Psa 51:17: "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise.": What it is set against: "For you will not delight in sacrifice, or I would give it; you will not be pleased with a burnt offering" (51:16); What comes before: "Deliver me from bloodguiltiness" (51:14). 15468.text: A reversal, and a boast turned around: "Let the lowly brother boast in his exaltation, and the rich in his humiliation, because like a flower of the grass he will pass away" (Jam 1:9–10); "God chose what is low and despised in the world, even things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are, so that no human being might boast in the presence of God … 'Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord'" (1Cor 1:28–31); I read: in both, the low is where God's choosing and lifting are seen. The boast is moved from what one has to what God does. The rich man's "humiliation" is something to boast in, because it tells him the truth: he passes like grass.

15680.text: The verses do not name humility as a feeling. 16491.text: 13. Cross-cutting observations for Batch E [Claude reading]: Relating to God engages the whole inner seat, and the texts say so by formula.; "With all your heart and with all your soul" governs: serving (Deu 10:12; Jos 22:5); keeping the law and renewing the covenant (2Ki 23:3; 2Ch 34:31; Deu 30:10); loving after circumcision of heart (Deu 30:6); praying and returning (1Ki 8:48); being tested (Deu 13:3); "With my whole heart" governs thanks, praise, crying and seeking.; The formula also appears of God (Jer 32:41).; The heart is where the relation to God is located, examined and known.; It prays without voice (1Sa 1:13) and cries (Lam 2:18).; It holds the law (Psa 37:31) and trusts (Psa 28:7).; It believes (Rom 10:10) and is circumcised (Deu 30:6).; It is the organ God tests (§8.1). Knowing hearts is the ground of God's forgiveness (1Ki 8:39) and of his giving the Spirit (Act 15:8).; Where heart and lips diverge, the lips do not count (Hos 7:14; Isa 29:13).; The soul is the self in address. It is spoken to by its owner ("Bless the Lord, O my soul"; "Why are you cast down, O my soul"), and asked to be spoken to by God ("Say to my soul, 'I am your salvation'", Psa 35:3). It is also the life that is: asked for (Est 7:3; 1Ki 17:21); asked to die (1Ki 19:4; Jon 4:8); redeemed, ransomed and atoned for (§9.1, §11.1); delivered or lost (§11.3); The human spirit is most active in this batch.; It prays and sings apart from the mind (1Co 14:14–16).; It serves (Rom 1:9) and worships in spirit (Joh 4:23–24).; It rejoices in the Savior (Luk 1:47) and is renewed (Eze 36:26; Eph 4:23).; It receives the benediction "grace be with your spirit".; At death it is the part committed to God (Psa 31:5; Luk 23:46; Act 7:59; Mat 27:50).; Its complaint voices anguish (Job 7:11), and its brokenness blocks hearing (Exo 6:9).; The divine Spirit relates to God on the person's behalf.; It cries "Abba" in the heart (Gal 4:6) and intercedes within the searched heart (Rom 8:26–27).; It bears witness (Heb 10:15) and writes on hearts (2Co 3:3).; It circumcises the heart (Rom 2:29) and renews (Tit 3:5).; It gives faith and gifts (1Co 12:9; Gal 3:2) and speaks through the prophet (2Sa 23:2).; It can itself be tested (Act 5:9), resisted (Act 7:51) and outraged (Heb 10:29).; Other spirits relate to God too, and are judged by that relation.

16492.text: 13. Cross-cutting observations for Batch E [Claude reading]: Unclean spirits recognise the Son of God (Mar 3:11) and obey him (Mar 1:27).; Spirits either confess Jesus come in the flesh or are "the spirit of the antichrist" (1Jo 4:2–3).; They must be tested (1Jo 4:1), and the spirit of error stands against the Spirit of truth (1Jo 4:6).; The Lord can dispatch a lying spirit (1Ki 22:23). Ministering spirits serve (Heb 1:14).; Flesh in relating to God: "All flesh" is humanity as it comes to God: all flesh comes in prayer (Psa 65:2), sees salvation and glory (Luk 3:6; Isa 40:5), and blesses (Psa 145:21).; Covenant is cut in the flesh, and its inner counterpart is the circumcised heart (§7.2).; Flesh vs spirit as powers: Isa 31:3; Joh 6:63; 1Co 5:5; Jer 17:5.; The "life of the flesh is in the blood" (Lev 17:11) is the ground of atonement.; God is shown with his own heart and soul in these relations: his soul avenges (Jer 5:9) and he swears by it (Amo 6:8); he acts with all his heart and soul (Jer 32:41); he wishes for a heart in his people (Deu 5:29); his heart recoils in compassion (Hos 11:8); his soul delights in the servant (Isa 42:1); he gives up the beloved of his soul (Jer 12:7); the priest acts according to his heart and soul (1Sa 2:35); Speech and the heart. The heart speaks inwardly ("in the heart", §1.3), is spoken to ("to the heart" = comfort, §1.4), and its speech either matches the mouth or is betrayed by it. Hebrew prayer is an act of the heart that may or may not reach the lips.; Fringe worth keeping: *kāvôd* as the inner self (§3.2) — a possible inner-being term outside M47; the soul asked to die (§2); the double portion of another's spirit (2Ki 2:9); the dying soul naming a child and the returning spirit naming a spring (§1.8); Isaac's soul giving the blessing (§12); Qoheleth testing his own heart (Ecc 2:1); the Gentile's heart-and-conscience law-court (Rom 2:15); the flesh-then-breath sequence of the dry bones (Eze 37:6–8); "gain the whole world and forfeit his soul" (Mat 16:26); "transgression speaks [as an oracle] deep in his heart" (Psa 36:1); the heart with "highways to Zion" (Psa 84:5); "absent in body … present in spirit" (Col 2:5)

16727.text: 11. Cross-cutting observations for Batch D [Claude reading]: Conscience is the NT's named moral-awareness faculty. It can be clear, pure, good, evil, defiled, seared, weak or wounded. It testifies (2Co 1:12; Rom 9:1) and is purified by Christ's blood (Heb 9:14). It is frequently paired with the heart (1Ti 1:5; Heb 10:22).; The OT does this work with the heart: "David's heart struck him" (2Sa 24:10); "my heart does not reproach me" (Job 27:6).; The Levitical "realizes his guilt" (Lev 5) describes the same moment without naming an organ.; The heart deceives itself and is the source of evil.; It deceives its owner: Jer 17:9; Obd 3; Isa 44:20.; Evil comes from it: Gen 6:5; Mat 15:19; Luk 6:45.; Its evil hides behind speech: Psa 28:3; 41:6; Pro 26:23–25.; Pride deceives the heart that holds it (Obd 3), linking M08 and M14.; Flesh carries on from Batch C (§11.5).; OT: flesh is the ritual body and meat — clean or unclean, holy or tainted.; NT Pauline: flesh is the seat of sin (Rom 7–8; Gal 5:19) and the ground of false boasting (Phili 3:3).; Positive NT uses remain: "holy … in his body of flesh" (Col 1:22); "bodies as a living sacrifice" (Rom 12:1).; Wind and breath are the image of moral emptiness: iniquity takes us away like wind (Isa 64:6); the wicked are chaff (Psa 1:4); "wind and lies" (Mic 2:11); idols with no breath (Jer 10:14); the *hevel* + *rûaḥ* refrain (Ecc); Only the messianic "breath of his lips" (Isa 11:4) and the breath that conveys the Holy Spirit (Joh 20:22) are active and effective.; Fringe worth keeping: *nephesh* = corpse as the defiling body (§8.2); the "high heart" that is pride or courage depending on direction (2Ch 17:6 vs 2Ch 32:25); the heart that strikes or does not reproach — pre-conscience (§3.3, §9.5); sin against one's own soul (§3.2); the servant's soul as guilt offering (§3.6); lies that kill and keep alive souls (Eze 13:19); the spirit of jealousy that comes whether or not the defilement is real (Num 5:14); false humility of the flesh (Col 2:18, 23); the thorn in the flesh against conceit (2Co 12:7); Eliab misreading David's heart (1Sa 17:28); "Is your heart true to my heart as mine is to yours?" (2Ki 10:15)

16751.text: Ben-hadad and the prophet's parable. Context read: 1Ki 20:31–43.; "Perhaps he will spare your life" (31) → "Please, let me live" → "Does he still live? He is my brother" (32); The disguised prophet: "Guard this man; if … he is missing, your life shall be for his life, or else you shall pay a talent of silver" (39); "your life shall be for his life, and your people for his people" (42) → Ahab "went to his house vexed and sullen" (43; the same phrase as 21:4 — Batch F §7); [Claude reading] A life has a price in silver in the parable, but not in the verdict. 16782.text: 2.2 The price of a life, again: "The ransom of a man's life is his wealth, but a poor man hears no threat" (Pro 13:8); "each shall give a ransom for his life … The rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less … to make atonement for your lives" (Exo 30:12–16; context read) → Batch D; Batch E; "your life shall be for his life, or else you shall pay a talent of silver" (1Ki 20:39) → §1.4; Satan: "Skin for skin! All that a man has he will give for his life" (Job 2:4) → "only spare [*guard*] his life" (2:6). Context read: Job 2:3–7.; "they have devoured human lives; they have taken treasure" (Eze 22:25); [Claude reading] Batch G §5.4 read Mic 6:7 and Mat 16:26 as a refusal to set any price on the soul. This batch shows the law and the narratives do set a price, and state it: a ransom in wealth (Pro 13:8); a half-shekel that is equal for every life (Exo 30:15); a talent of silver in a parable that turns into "life for life" (1Ki 20:39–42); Satan's axiom (Job 2:4) is that a man will give everything for his *nephesh*. The difference from G §5.4 is the direction of the transaction: a life can be ransomed within the covenant, but a soul cannot be bought back from God (Mat 16:26). See §R-V.

17174.text: 11. Cross-cutting observations for Batch C [Claude reading]: The soul is the desiring self. In the OT, *nephesh* is the ordinary subject of "want / crave / long / thirst", from appetite for meat (Deu 12:20) to thirst for God (Psa 42:1–2). The same *nephesh* is the life that enemies seek (§7.5) and the life that is precious (§1.7). Desire and vitality are one word.; The heart is where orientation is set, held, divided or hardened. It plans, forms intentions, resolves, seeks, turns, is whole or not whole, and is stubborn or hardened. Many of these are expressed as setting / directing / inclining the heart (1Sa 7:3; Jos 24:23; 2Ch 19:3; 30:19). This extends Batch B's "attention = setting the heart" into will.; The human spirit carries energy and disposition, more than choice. It is "moved" to give (Exo 35:21), "fervent" (Rom 12:11), "willing" against weak flesh (Mat 26:41), patient or proud (Ecc 7:8), ruled (Pro 16:32), hardened with the heart (Deu 2:30), not faithful (Psa 78:8), and crushed or contrite (Psa 34:18; 51:17). Planning and choosing are rarely predicated of the human spirit [observation, not a count].; Heart and spirit are paired in the orientation verses (Exo 35:21; Deu 2:30; Psa 51:17; 78:8; Isa 57:15; Eze 11:19; 36:26). Heart and soul are paired in the "all your heart and all your soul" formula for seeking and returning (Deu 4:29; 1Ki 8:48; 2Ch 15:12).; Flesh changes role across the corpus.; OT: flesh longs and faints for God with the soul (Psa 63:1; 84:2). The "heart of flesh" is God's gift (Eze 36:26).; NT: flesh is the main subject of wrong desire (Gal 5:16–17; 1Jo 2:16), set against the Spirit and the soul (1Pe 2:11) and weak beside a willing spirit (Mat 26:41).; 2Co 3:3 ("tablets of fleshly hearts") keeps the OT positive use inside the NT.; God's Spirit relates to orientation as giver and as the one resisted.; Giver: good Spirit leading (Psa 143:10), patience (Gal 5:22), hope (Rom 5:5; 15:13), received on repentance (Act 2:38).; Resisted: rebelled against and grieved (Isa 63:10), disregarded (1Th 4:8), bypassed in plans (Isa 30:1).; The Spirit also desires against the flesh (Gal 5:17) and wills (1Co 12:11).

19403.text: Joshua 24:15 — "choose this day whom you will serve": Joshua does not open with the choice. He opens with eleven verses in which the Lord speaks of what *he* did: *"I took your father Abraham from beyond the River"*; *"I brought you out"*; *"I gave them into your hand"*; *"it was not by your sword or by your bow"* (v3–12); The recital starts where the people's story started: *"your fathers lived beyond the Euphrates … and they served other gods"* (v2). Before Israel ever chose, the Lord had already taken Abraham out from among those gods. The choice put to the people at Shechem comes at the end of that history, not at the start of it.; The choice is not whether to serve. Serving is taken for granted: the fathers served gods beyond the River, and the Amorites serve the gods of the land. The only question is *whom*. So the choosing is a choice of master.; It begins in the eyes: *"if it is evil in your eyes to serve the Lord, choose this day"*. Joshua treats the people's own view of what is good and evil as where the choice starts, and he leaves it open to them. He even names the alternatives for them. Then he makes his own choice in front of them, before they answer: *"as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord."*; The people choose from memory: *"it is the Lord our God who brought us … up from the land of Egypt, … and who did those great signs in our sight"* (v17). Their choosing rests on what they saw.; Joshua's reply is not what a speaker would say if he only wanted agreement: *"You are not able to serve the Lord, for he is a holy God. He is a jealous God"* (v19). Choosing and being able to carry the choice out are not the same thing, and Joshua says so plainly. The people insist, *"No, but we will serve the Lord"* (v21).; At that point the choice turns back on the one who made it: *"You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen the Lord"* (v22). Once spoken, a choice becomes a testimony the chooser will be held to.; It also exposes what is still in the house: *"Then put away the foreign gods that are among you, and incline your heart to the Lord"* (v23). The people have just chosen the Lord, yet the foreign gods are still among them. So the choice spoken with the mouth has to be followed by two things: putting something away; an inner turning, the heart inclined (H5186, "to stretch, bend")

19405.text: Psalm 119:30 — "I have chosen the way of faithfulness": This verse sits in the stanza that begins *"My soul clings to the dust; give me life according to your word!"* (v25). Two verses before it the psalmist says *"My soul melts away for sorrow; strengthen me according to your word!"* (v28). The person who chooses here is low and spent, not standing strong over the options.; Around the choosing the psalmist is mostly asking: *"teach me"*; *"Make me understand"*; *"strengthen me"*; *"Put false ways far from me"* (v26–29); The false way is not refused by his own strength alone. He asks God to put it at a distance. Then he states the choice: *"I have chosen the way of faithfulness; I set your rules before me"* (v30). The choosing is joined at once to keeping something in view: he puts the rules in front of himself, where he can see them.; The next verse uses the same word as the first verse of the stanza: v25: *"My soul clings to the dust"* (H1692); v31: *"I cling to your testimonies, O Lord"* (H1692); The verb is the same, and what it holds on to has changed. I read the choice in v30 as the turn between the two: the soul that was clinging to the dust now clings to the testimonies. The stanza places the verbs in this order; it does not name the change.; The stanza ends forward-looking, with a condition: *"I will run in the way of your commandments when you enlarge my heart!"* (v32). The choice has been made, but running in the chosen way waits on something God does to the heart.

19406.text: Isaiah 65:12 — "chose what I did not delight in": This is an oracle. It opens with God, not with the people: *"I was ready to be sought by those who did not ask for me … I said, “Here I am, here I am,”"* (v1); *"I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people, who walk in a way that is not good, following their own devices"* (v2); The wrong choosing in v12 is made in front of a God who is calling and holding out his hands.; The oracle shows what they turned to instead: sacrifices *"in gardens"*, sitting *"in tombs"*, eating *"pig’s flesh"* (v3–4); a pride that says *"do not come near me, for I am too holy for you"* (v5); they *"forget my holy mountain"* and *"set a table for Fortune and fill cups of mixed wine for Destiny"* (v11); They put their trust in luck and fate.; The answer turns on their own word: *"I will destine you to the sword"* (v12). In Hebrew, "Destiny" (Meni, H4507) and "destine" (manah, H4487) come from the same root. They poured cups for Destiny, and the Lord destines them. What they chose to trust becomes the form their judgement takes.; The verse then gives the reason, and the reason is in the inner being: *"because, when I called, you did not answer; when I spoke, you did not listen, but you did what was evil in my eyes and chose what I did not delight in."* The choosing does not stand alone. It is the far end of not answering and not listening. When they turned away from the voice calling them, that was already a choice, and choosing what God does not delight in is where it ends.; There is a phrase to set beside Joshua 24. There, the choice turned on what was *"evil in your eyes"*. Here they *"did what was evil in my eyes"*. The measure has moved from their eyes to God's, and his delight is the standard their choice is judged by.; In the same oracle the word "chosen" is used of the others: *"my chosen shall possess it"* (v9); *"You shall leave your name to my chosen for a curse"* (v15); So in one passage there are those who chose what God did not delight in, and those God calls *"my chosen"*. The outcome sets the two side by side and reaches the inner being on both sides: *"my servants shall sing for gladness of heart, but you shall cry out for pain of heart and shall wail for breaking of spirit"* (v14). The choice ends in the heart and spirit of the one who made it.

19407.text: "In whose eyes": Jos 24:15 has *"evil in your eyes"*, and Isa 65:12 has *"evil in my eyes"*.

19496.text: Joy and singing. *"So he brought his people out with joy, his chosen ones with singing"* (Psa 105:43), after *"he remembered his holy promise"* (105:42).

19497.text: Not fearing. *"Fear not, O Jacob my servant, Jeshurun whom I have chosen"* (Isa 44:2). The ground is who chose him: *"the Lord who made you, who formed you from the womb and will help you"*.

19500.text: Be strong, and do it. *"the Lord has chosen you to build a house for the sanctuary; be strong and do it"* (1Ch 28:10). The strength is first a strength *"in keeping my commandments"* (28:7). Fear is answered: *"Do not be afraid and do not be dismayed, for the Lord God, even my God, is with you"* (28:20).

19506.text: Faith, knowing and the truth: Faith, and knowing the truth, are named for the chosen in five of these verses: *"for the sake of the faith of God's elect and their knowledge of the truth, which accords with godliness, in hope of eternal life"* (Tit 1:1–2); *"rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom, which he has promised to those who love him"* (Jam 2:5); *"that you may know and believe me and understand that I am he"* (Isa 43:10); *"belief in the truth"* (2Th 2:13); *"having the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope to which he has called you"* (Eph 1:18), a prayer for people already chosen; Faith is shown in what it does: *"So also faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead"* (Jam 2:17). In the chapter of Titus 1:1 the opposite is described: *"They profess to know God, but they deny him by their works"* (Tit 1:16).

19507.text: Before whom: The chosen live before God's sight, not others'. David answers Michal, who measured him by *"the eyes of his servants' female servants"* (2Sa 6:20): *"It was before the Lord, who chose me"*, and *"I will be abased in your eyes"* (6:21–22). The purpose of the choosing in Ephesians is to be holy and blameless *"before him"* (Eph 1:4).

19512.text: The heart's own wish refused. David, chosen, was not allowed to build what was in his heart (1Ch 28:2–4).

19519.text: Those of one mind with the beast. The kings *"are of one mind, and they hand over their power and authority to the beast"*, and against them *"those with him are called and chosen and faithful"* (Rev 17:13–14).

19521.text: Choosing a person.; God chooses *"before the foundation of the world"*, before anything in the person (Eph 1:4). He chooses people who are blind and deaf (Isa 43:8, 10), and the poor (Jam 2:5).; People choose by what is already seen and said: *"men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom"* (Act 6:3).; *Why:* who chooses. With God, the inner life is the purpose of the choosing. With people, it is the measure.

19522.text: Holiness.; It is the purpose of the choosing: *"that we should be holy and blameless before him"* (Eph 1:4).; It is a name the chosen already carry, while the inner qualities are still to be put on: *"as God's chosen ones, holy and beloved"* (Col 3:12).; *Why:* the verses do not say. I set them side by side.

19523.text: The chosen people.; They are brought out *"with joy … with singing"* (Psa 105:43).; They despise the land, with no faith in the promise (Psa 106:24).; *Why:* Psalm 105 tells of what God did, and gives none of the people's failures (it has *"none among his tribes who stumbled"*, 105:37). Psalm 106 tells of what the people did. The text does not join the two psalms.

19525.text: God's choosing and a person's belief (2Th 2:13). Both are named in one sentence. How they fit is not said.
