19543.text: Led to: Joshua recounts what the Lord gave: *"a land on which you had not labored"* (v13). Then he calls on them: *"fear the Lord and serve him in sincerity and in faithfulness. Put away the gods"* (v14). The choice is put to them on one condition: *"if it is evil in your eyes to serve the Lord, choose this day whom you will serve"* (v15).

19544.text: Choice: Joshua chooses first: *"as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord"* (v15).; The people choose the Lord, giving the reason from what he did: *"it is the Lord our God who brought us … up from the land of Egypt"* (v17); *"Therefore we also will serve the Lord, for he is our God"* (v18).; Joshua answers *"You are not able to serve the Lord, for he is a holy God"* (v19). They repeat the choice: *"No, but we will serve the Lord"* (v21).

19545.text: Outcome: The choice binds them as its own witness: *"You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen the Lord"*; *"We are witnesses"* (v22).; It calls for an inner act: *"put away the foreign gods … and incline your heart to the Lord"* (v23).; *"his voice we will obey"* (v24). A covenant, statutes and rules are made, and a stone is set up as *"a witness against you, lest you deal falsely with your God"* (v25–27).; The warning is part of the outcome: *"If you forsake the Lord … he will turn and do you harm"* (v20).

19550.text: Choice: *"what they said pleased the whole gathering, and they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, and Philip …"* (v5). The pleasure is the gathering's response to the twelve's word, and the choosing follows it.

19553.text: Choice: *"it seemed good to the apostles and the elders, with the whole church, to choose men from among them and send them to Antioch"*. The men are *"Judas called Barsabbas, and Silas"* (v22).; In the letter: *"it has seemed good to us, having come to one accord, to choose men and send them"* (v25).; The same verb then carries the content of the letter: *"it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us"* (v28).

19559.text: Choice: the slave's: *"in the place that he shall choose within one of your towns, wherever it suits him"* (v16).

19560.text: Outcome: Given as law, not narrated: *"He shall dwell with you, in your midst … You shall not wrong him"* (v16). Israel is to honour the choice and not hand him back: *"You shall not give up to his master"* (v15).

19562.text: Choice: *"I have chosen the way of faithfulness; I set your rules before me"* (v30).

19564.text: Led to: The Lord's character: *"Good and upright is the Lord; therefore he instructs sinners in the way"* (v8).; The person's fear: *"Who is the man who fears the Lord? Him will he instruct in the way that he should choose"* (v12).; The psalmist's own plea just before: *"pardon my guilt, for it is great"* (v11).

19567.text: Choice: *"who keep my Sabbaths, who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant"* (v4). What is chosen is measured by what pleases the Lord.

19569.text: Led to: *"you who forsake the Lord, who forget my holy mountain, who set a table for Fortune"* (v11).; *"when I called, you did not answer; when I spoke, you did not listen"* (v12).

19570.text: Choice: *"you did what was evil in my eyes and chose what I did not delight in"* (v12).

19571.text: Outcome: *"I will destine you to the sword"* (v12).; *"my servants shall eat, but you shall be hungry … my servants shall rejoice, but you shall be put to shame"* (v13).; The outcome reaches the inner being: *"you shall cry out for pain of heart and shall wail for breaking of spirit"* (v14).; *"You shall leave your name to my chosen for a curse"* (v15).

19572.text: Led to: Set against the one the Lord looks to: *"he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word"* (v2).; Their offerings are named as like killing a man or offering pig's blood (v3).; v4 gives the same ground as Isa 65:12: *"when I called, no one answered, when I spoke, they did not listen"*.

19573.text: Choice: *"These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations"* (v3). The choosing and the soul's delight stand side by side. *"chose that in which I did not delight"* (v4).

19574.text: Outcome: The Lord answers with a choice of his own: *"I also will choose harsh treatment for them and bring their fears upon them"* (v4). Their own fears are what comes on them. To those who tremble: *"it is they who shall be put to shame"* (v5).

19576.text: Choice: *"the oaks that you desired … the gardens that you have chosen"* (v29).

19577.text: Outcome: *"they shall be ashamed … you shall blush"* (v29).; They become like what they chose: *"like an oak whose leaf withers, and like a garden without water"* (v30).; *"the strong shall become tinder … both of them shall burn together, with none to quench them"* (v31).

19578.text: Led to: In Eliphaz's account: *"you are doing away with the fear of God and hindering meditation before God"* (v4); *"your iniquity teaches your mouth"* (v5).

19579.text: Choice: *"you choose the tongue of the crafty"* (v5).

19582.text: Choice: *"Take care; do not turn to iniquity, for this you have chosen rather than affliction"* (v21). Elihu says Job has chosen iniquity over affliction, which v15 calls the means by which God opens the ear.

19585.text: Choice: Urged, together: *"Let us choose what is right; let us know among ourselves what is good"* (v4).

19587.text: Led to: Elihu's question whether anyone has said to God *"I will not offend any more; teach me what I do not see"* (v31–32).; *"Will he then make repayment to suit you, because you reject it?"* (v33).

19588.text: Choice: Laid on Job: *"For you must choose, and not I; therefore declare what you know"* (v33).

19590.text: Choice: Forbidden: *"Do not envy a man of violence and do not choose any of his ways"* (v31).

19593.text: Choice: Urged: *"Take my instruction instead of silver, and knowledge rather than choice gold"* (v10). Knowledge is set above the gold that is itself called "choice".

19595.text: Choice: Urged as a value: *"How much better to get wisdom than gold! To get understanding is to be chosen rather than silver"* (v16).

19597.text: Outcome: The knowing serves as a measure of time: *"before the boy knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good, the land whose two kings you dread will be deserted"* (v16).; *"the king of Assyria"* follows (v17).; Ahaz's own refusal in v12 is the occasion of the whole sign. The verses do not connect it to the child's refusing.

19598.text: What the verse gives as the ground: the Lord's acts: 1 (v17–18) and 8 (v8); God putting care in the heart: 5 (v16); what pleased the gathering: 3; Barzillai's age and faded discernment: 2 (v35); not listening: 10, 11

19599.text: F2. Pro 8:10 (entry 18). The choosing word describes the gold (*"choice gold"*), not the person's choosing. Knowledge is preferred over it. It sits in §2a as the "object" of choice. Should it stay there, or move with the "Choice: the best" group?

19600.text: F3. Isa 7:15–16 (entry 20). The verses name a capacity to choose, not a choice made. It stays in §2a as "ground", but it is a different kind of entry from the others.

19601.text: F4. Isa 1:29 (entry 12). The reading of the oaks and gardens as places of other worship is marked "I read". The verse names only oaks and gardens.

19602.text: 2 Samuel 6:21: "and I will celebrate before the Lord": The chapter is the bringing up of the ark. It opens in celebration: *"David and all the house of Israel were celebrating before the Lord, with songs and lyres"* (v5). Then Uzzah takes hold of the ark and *"the anger of the Lord was kindled against Uzzah"* (v7). David's inner state turns three times in three verses: *"David was angry because the Lord had broken out against Uzzah"* (v8); *"David was afraid of the Lord that day, and he said, "How can the ark of the Lord come to me?""* (v9); *"So David was not willing to take the ark of the Lord into the city of David"* (v10); What brings him back is hearing that *"The Lord has blessed the household of Obed-edom"* (v12). He brings the ark up *"with rejoicing"*, and *"David danced before the Lord with all his might"* (v14).; Michal sees this from the window and *"she despised him in her heart"* (v16). The contempt is inward first. Her words come out only when he arrives (v20). Her measure is the eyes of others: *"uncovering himself today before the eyes of his servants' female servants"* (v20).; David's answer: *"It was before the Lord, who chose me above your father and above all his house, to appoint me as prince over Israel, the people of the Lord—and I will celebrate before the Lord"* (v21). "Celebrate" is the same word as *"celebrating"* in v5 (H7832). The celebration that stopped at Uzzah's death has come back, and David names the ground: he was chosen. He also names before whom he celebrates. Michal spoke of the servants' eyes. David speaks of the Lord.; He does not defend his dignity. He goes further: *"I will make myself yet more contemptible than this, and I will be abased in your eyes"* (v22). He accepts being lowered in her eyes. Her contempt does not move him, because he answers to a different measure.; The choosing is set against Michal's own house: *"above your father and above all his house"*. I read the reply as answering her contempt with the fact of the choosing. The verse names the house of Saul directly. The chapter closes on Michal: *"Michal the daughter of Saul had no child to the day of her death"* (v23). The text does not give a cause.

19603.text: 1 Chronicles 28:10: "the Lord has chosen you … be strong and do it": David speaks to the whole assembly, then to Solomon. He begins with his own heart and its refusal: *"I had it in my heart to build a house of rest for the ark"* (v2), *"But God said to me, 'You may not build a house for my name'"* (v3). The man who says *"the Lord God of Israel chose me"* (v4) was refused what was in his heart. Being chosen did not give David everything he intended.; He speaks of his own choosing in inner terms: *"among my father's sons he took pleasure in me to make me king"* (v4, H7521). Then Solomon: *"I have chosen him to be my son, and I will be his father"* (v6).; The promise to Solomon is conditional: *"I will establish his kingdom forever if he continues strong in keeping my commandments and my rules"* (v7). The words to Solomon follow from that condition: *"know the God of your father and serve him with a whole heart and with a willing mind, for the Lord searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought"* (v9); *"If you seek him, he will be found by you, but if you forsake him, he will cast you off forever"* (v9); *"Be careful now, for the Lord has chosen you to build a house for the sanctuary; be strong and do it"* (v10); "Strong" in v10 is the same word as *"continues strong in keeping"* in v7 (H2388G). The strength asked of the chosen man is first a strength in keeping. "Be careful" in v10 is the verb "see" (H7200H).; The chosen man's inner being is named on every side: the heart, whole; the mind, willing (H5315G, the soul); every plan and thought, searched by the Lord; Being chosen does not end the searching. The same verse that calls him chosen holds out *"cast you off forever"*.; David repeats the charge at the end with its reason: *"Be strong and courageous and do it. Do not be afraid and do not be dismayed, for the Lord God, even my God, is with you. He will not leave you or forsake you"* (v20). In v9, Solomon is told the Lord will forsake him if he forsakes the Lord. In v20 he is told the Lord will not forsake him until the work is done. Both are said to the one man.

19604.text: Psalm 65:4: "We shall be satisfied with the goodness of your house": The psalm opens with prayer and with sin: *"O you who hear prayer, to you shall all flesh come"* (v2); *"When iniquities prevail against me, you atone for our transgressions"* (v3); The verse comes straight after the atoning: *"Blessed is the one you choose and bring near, to dwell in your courts! We shall be satisfied with the goodness of your house, the holiness of your temple!"* (v4). Being chosen is set with being brought near and dwelling. The response is satisfaction (H7646), and what satisfies is *"the goodness of your house"*. The satisfaction is not in the chosen person; it is in what is in God's house.; The speaker moves from *"me"* (v3) to *"we"* (v4). The one chosen is spoken of in the singular, and the satisfaction is spoken in the plural.; The psalm then widens beyond the chosen. God is *"the hope of all the ends of the earth"* (v5), and *"those who dwell at the ends of the earth are in awe at your signs"* (v8). The land itself is given voice at the end: *"they shout and sing together for joy"* (v13). The joy of the chosen in v4 is one part of a psalm that ends with all of creation rejoicing. The verse does not say the chosen have the joy alone.

19606.text: Psalm 105:43: "his chosen ones with singing": Psalm 105 is a call to remember. It is addressed to the chosen: *"Remember the wondrous works that he has done … O offspring of Abraham, his servant, children of Jacob, his chosen ones!"* (v5–6). It starts with the heart: *"let the hearts of those who seek the Lord rejoice!"* (v3).; The psalm's reason is God's own remembering: *"He remembers his covenant forever"* (v8); *"For he remembered his holy promise, and Abraham, his servant"* (v42); The verse follows straight on: *"So he brought his people out with joy, his chosen ones with singing"* (v43). The joy and singing are set on the people brought out. They come with being brought out, and the bringing out comes from God remembering his promise. The chosen are told to remember (v5) because he remembered (v8, v42).; On the way there the psalm tells one man's inward testing: *"His feet were hurt with fetters … until what he had said came to pass, the word of the Lord tested him"* (v18–19). That man was Joseph, sent ahead of the chosen.; Psalm 105 tells nothing of the people's failures. It has *"none among his tribes who stumbled"* (v37). Its last verse states the purpose of the whole: *"that they might keep his statutes and observe his laws"* (v45).

19607.text: Psalm 106:5: "that I may rejoice in the gladness of your nation": Psalm 106 follows 105 and tells the same history from the other side. I read the two side by side because they stand together; neither refers to the other.; The speaker asks to be included: *"Remember me, O Lord, when you show favor to your people; help me when you save them, that I may look upon the prosperity of your chosen ones, that I may rejoice in the gladness of your nation, that I may glory with your inheritance"* (v4–5). He does not claim the chosen ones' gladness. He asks to look upon it and to share it. "Gladness" here (H8057) is the same word as David's *"rejoicing"* in 2 Samuel 6:12.; He then confesses at once: *"Both we and our fathers have sinned; we have committed iniquity; we have done wickedness"* (v6). The rest of the psalm is the chosen people's inner failure, named act by act: *"did not consider your wondrous works; they did not remember the abundance of your steadfast love"* (v7); *"Then they believed his words; they sang his praise. But they soon forgot his works; they did not wait for his counsel"* (v12–13); *"they had a wanton craving in the wilderness"* (v14); *"men in the camp were jealous of Moses and Aaron"* (v16); *"They forgot God, their Savior"* (v21); *"Then they despised the pleasant land, having no faith in his promise"* (v24); *"they were rebellious in their purposes"* (v43); "Despised" in v24 is H3988A, the same word as *"refuse the evil"* in Isaiah 7:15. The chosen people refused what they were given. "Faith" in v24 is H0539, the same word as *"believed"* in v12. The psalm has them believing, then forgetting, then without faith.; One of the chosen acts for the rest: *"had not Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach before him, to turn away his wrath"* (v23).; The psalm's turn is God's remembering, as in Psalm 105: *"he looked upon their distress, when he heard their cry. For their sake he remembered his covenant"* (v44–45). It ends with the chosen asking again for the joy of v5: *"gather us from among the nations, that we may give thanks to your holy name and glory in your praise"* (v47).

19608.text: Isaiah 43:10: "my servant whom I have chosen, that you may know and believe me and understand": The setting is a court. The nations are summoned: *"All the nations gather together … Let them bring their witnesses to prove them right"* (v9). Israel is brought out as the Lord's witness, and described as unfit for it: *"Bring out the people who are blind, yet have eyes, who are deaf, yet have ears!"* (v8).; Then: *"You are my witnesses," declares the Lord, "and my servant whom I have chosen, that you may know and believe me and understand that I am he"* (v10). The knowing, believing and understanding are the purpose of the choosing. They are not its ground. The chosen were blind and deaf when chosen. They were chosen in order to come to know.; This is the reverse of the order in §2a, where the child chooses *"when he knows how"* (Isa 7:15). There the knowing comes before the person's own choosing. Here, the knowing follows God's choosing of the person. Each verse states its own order.; What the chosen are to know is one thing: *"that I am he. Before me no god was formed"* (v10). The Lord's own witness follows: *"I declared and saved and proclaimed, when there was no strange god among you"* (v12).; The oracles that follow set the chosen beside those who make idols: The chosen people do not perceive what God is doing: *"Behold, I am doing a new thing; now it springs forth, do you not perceive it?"* (43:19). "Perceive" is the same word as "know" in v10 (H3045).; The idol-makers' witnesses *"neither see nor know"* (44:9).; Of the idol-maker himself: *"They know not, nor do they discern, for he has shut their eyes, so that they cannot see, and their hearts, so that they cannot understand"* (44:18). "Know" and "discern" are the same words as "know" and "understand" in 43:10 (H3045, H0995).; The chosen people are also accused: *"Yet you did not call upon me, O Jacob; but you have been weary of me, O Israel!"* (43:22); *"you have burdened me with your sins; you have wearied me with your iniquities"* (43:24). Then comes the answer: *"I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins"* (43:25).

19609.text: Isaiah 44:2: "Fear not, O Jacob my servant, Jeshurun whom I have chosen": The chapter opens directly after a threat: *"deliver Jacob to utter destruction and Israel to reviling"* (43:28). Then: *"But now hear, O Jacob my servant, Israel whom I have chosen!"* (44:1). The "fear not" comes right after the words of destruction.; The ground of not fearing is who the Lord is to the one chosen: *"the Lord who made you, who formed you from the womb and will help you: Fear not, O Jacob my servant, Jeshurun whom I have chosen"* (v2). He made, he formed, he will help, and he has chosen. The chosen person is not told to be brave. He is told who has chosen him.; What follows is given to the chosen one's offspring, and it reaches the inner being: *"I will pour my Spirit upon your offspring, and my blessing on your descendants"* (v3); *"This one will say, 'I am the Lord's,' another will call on the name of Jacob, and another will write on his hand, 'The Lord's'"* (v5); Those who are chosen come to name themselves as belonging to him.; The "fear not" comes again with a second ground: *"Fear not, nor be afraid; have I not told you from of old and declared it? And you are my witnesses!"* (v8). The second ground is having been told.; The idol-maker in the same chapter has no such ground. He cuts the wood himself and then prays to it: *"Deliver me, for you are my god!"* (v17). The text says *"he cannot deliver himself"* (v20). The chosen one is told: *"Remember these things, O Jacob … you will not be forgotten by me"* (v21), and *"return to me, for I have redeemed you"* (v22).

19610.text: What this verse shows of being chosen: The chosen person's fear is answered with who has chosen him: maker, former, helper.; It is answered again with what he has been told from of old.; Being chosen reaches the next generation: the Spirit poured out, and people naming themselves the Lord's.; The chosen one is called to remember, and is told he will not be forgotten.; Against the chosen stands the idol-maker, who picks his own wood and cannot deliver himself. The ESV has *"he chooses a cypress tree or an oak"* (v14), but the Hebrew there is "take" (H3947G), not the choose word.

19611.text: What the chosen are moved to: celebrating (2Sa 6:21); being strong in keeping (1Ch 28:7, 10); satisfaction in the goodness of God's house (Psa 65:4); joy and singing (Psa 105:43); gladness, which another asks to share (Psa 106:5); knowing, believing and understanding (Isa 43:10); not fearing (Isa 44:2); In 2Sa 6:21, 1Ch 28:10, Isa 43:10 and Isa 44:2 the verse names the being chosen as the ground or the reason. In Psa 65:4 the response follows the choosing in the same sentence. In Psa 105:43 and 106:5, "chosen ones" names the people whose joy it is; the verse does not make the choosing the cause.

19612.text: Being chosen comes before the inner act, not after it. In §2a, knowing, fear and teaching came before a person's own choosing (Isa 7:15; Psa 25:12). In Isaiah 43:10, God chooses first, and knowing is the purpose. The chosen were blind and deaf when chosen (43:8). In Psalm 65 they were chosen after their iniquity was atoned for (v3–4).

19614.text: The return is the Lord's remembering. He remembered his covenant at their cry (Psa 106:44–45). He remembered his promise and brought them out with joy (Psa 105:42–43). He blots out their sins and will not remember them (Isa 43:25). The chosen are called to remember in turn (Psa 105:5; Isa 44:21).

19615.text: Before whom. David celebrates *"before the Lord"* against Michal's measure of the servants' eyes (2Sa 6:20–22). This sits with §2a, "whose measure": the eyes that judge the choice.

19616.text: The chosen still go through anger, fear and refusal. David was angry, afraid and unwilling between the two celebrations (2Sa 6:8–10). His own heart's wish to build was refused, though he was chosen (1Ch 28:2–4).

19620.text: For batch 2: the 8 New Testament verses. In five of them (Eph 1:4, 2Th 2:13, Tit 1:1, Jam 2:5, 2Pe 1:10) the inner act is given as the purpose of the choosing, or as the call that follows it. Whether they keep the order seen in Isaiah 43:10, with the choosing first and the knowing after, is to be read from them.

19621.text: Numbers 17:5: "Thus I will make to cease from me the grumblings of the people of Israel": The verse closes a long dispute over who God has chosen. It begins in Numbers 16. Korah and 250 chiefs, *"chosen from the assembly, well-known men"* (16:2; *qārîʾ*, H7148, "called"), rise up: *"Why then do you exalt yourselves above the assembly of the Lord?"* (16:3). Moses answers with God's choosing: *"The one whom he chooses he will bring near to him"* (16:5), and *"the man whom the Lord chooses shall be the holy one"* (16:7).; Moses names what is underneath the complaint: *"is it too small a thing for you that the God of Israel has separated you … And would you seek the priesthood also?"* (16:9–10). What they already have is not enough. They seek more.; *"Therefore it is against the Lord that you and all your company have gathered together. What is Aaron that you grumble against him?"* (16:11). The grumbling at Aaron is against the Lord.; Psalm 106 names the same event with an inner word: *"When men in the camp were jealous of Moses and Aaron, the holy one of the Lord, the earth opened and swallowed up Dathan, and covered the company of Abiram"* (Psa 106:16–17).; Moses himself is *"very angry"* (16:15). The rebels are judged (16:31–35). The next day *"all the congregation of the people of Israel grumbled against Moses and against Aaron, saying, 'You have killed the people of the Lord'"* (16:41). A plague begins, and Aaron *"stood between the dead and the living, and the plague was stopped"* (16:48).; Then God settles it with the staffs: *"And the staff of the man whom I choose shall sprout. Thus I will make to cease from me the grumblings of the people of Israel, which they grumble against you"* (17:5). The grumbling is against Moses and Aaron, and God calls it *"from me"*. In v10 it is *"their grumblings against me"*. The staff is kept *"as a sign for the rebels, that you may make an end of their grumblings against me, lest they die"* (17:10).; The grumbling turns to terror: *"Behold, we perish, we are undone, we are all undone. Everyone who comes near … shall die. Are we all to perish?"* (17:12–13).; "Grumble" is *lûn* (H3885B). The verse shows it as spoken complaint. I read the inner side from the passage: the seeking of the priesthood (16:10), and the jealousy that Psalm 106:16 names.

19627.text: 2 Samuel 6:16: "and she despised him in her heart": This verse was read for §2b from David's side. Here it is read for Michal.; *"As the ark of the Lord came into the city of David, Michal the daughter of Saul looked out of the window and saw King David leaping and dancing before the Lord, and she despised him in her heart"* (v16).; "Despised" is *bāzâ* (*to despise*; H0959), and it is *"in her heart"*. The contempt is inward first. It does not come out until David comes home to bless his household: *"How the king of Israel honored himself today, uncovering himself today before the eyes of his servants' female servants, as one of the vulgar fellows shamelessly uncovers himself!"* (v20).; Her measure is honour before others: *"honored himself"*, *"before the eyes of his servants' female servants"*. The joy she despises is joy *"before the Lord"* (v16).; David's answer brings in the choosing: *"It was before the Lord, who chose me above your father and above all his house"* (v21). The chapter names Michal *"the daughter of Saul"* three times (v16, v20, v23). I read the naming as setting her contempt in the house that was passed over. The text does not say this was her reason.; The same word, *bāzâ*, is the word in Isaiah 49:7, *"one deeply despised"*, set against the Lord's choosing (below).

19629.text: Psalm 106:5: "that I may rejoice in the gladness of your nation, that I may glory with your inheritance": This verse was read for §2b for the gladness of the chosen. Here it is read for the one who asks to share it.; *"Remember me, O Lord, when you show favor to your people; help me when you save them, that I may look upon the prosperity of your chosen ones, that I may rejoice in the gladness of your nation, that I may glory with your inheritance"* (v4–5).; The psalmist does not claim the gladness. He asks to be remembered so that he may share it. "Rejoice" is *śāmaḥ* (H8055). "Glory" is *hālal* (*to boast*; H1984H). His joy is to be joy *with* the chosen.; He asks it while confessing: *"Both we and our fathers have sinned; we have committed iniquity; we have done wickedness"* (v6). The rest of the psalm shows what the chosen people did (v7–43).

19635.text: Proverbs 10:20: "The tongue of the righteous is choice silver; the heart of the wicked is of little worth": "Choice" is *bāḥar* (H0977) as a description: tried, refined silver. No one chooses in the verse. The proverbs around it are about speech: *"The one who conceals hatred has lying lips"* (v18), *"whoever restrains his lips is prudent"* (v19), *"The lips of the righteous feed many"* (v21).; The researcher ruled on Proverbs 8:10 (F2) that it is not HIB as choosing, because "choice" describes the gold. The same holds here: "choice" describes the tongue.; The heart is in the verse, weighed: *"of little worth"*. It is set against the tongue of the righteous.

19639.text: Isaiah 58:5: "Is such the fast that I choose, a day for a person to humble himself?": Here the inner act is what is weighed by God's choosing. The chapter opens on people who look devout: *"Yet they seek me daily and delight to know my ways, as if they were a nation that did righteousness … they delight to draw near to God"* (v2); *"'Why have we fasted, and you see it not? Why have we humbled ourselves, and you take no knowledge of it?'"* (v3); The answer is about what is going on alongside the fast: *"Behold, in the day of your fast you seek your own pleasure, and oppress all your workers. Behold, you fast only to quarrel and to fight and to hit with a wicked fist"* (v3–4).; Then: *"Is such the fast that I choose, a day for a person to humble himself? Is it to bow down his head like a reed, and to spread sackcloth and ashes under him? Will you call this a fast, and a day acceptable to the Lord?"* (v5).; "Humble himself" in v5 is *ʿānâ* (*to afflict*; H6031B) with the soul (H5315I), the same phrase as *"humbled ourselves"* in v3. The self-humbling of the soul is what they offered. God asks whether that is what he chooses.; What he does choose is turned outward: *"Is not this the fast that I choose: to loose the bonds of wickedness, to undo the straps of the yoke, to let the oppressed go free, and to break every yoke? Is it not to share your bread with the hungry … and not to hide yourself from your own flesh?"* (v6–7).; "Delight" in v2 (twice) is *ḥāpēṣ* (H2654A). It is the same word as *"chose that in which I did not delight"* in Isaiah 66:4, read in §2a. In v3 *"your own pleasure"* is the noun from the same root (H2656).

19640.text: What this verse shows of others around the choosing: A person's inner act, the humbling of the soul, is weighed by what God chooses.; The self-humbling, done while seeking one's own pleasure and oppressing others, is not what he chooses (v3–5).; What he chooses is turned toward others: freeing, sharing, not hiding from one's own flesh (v6–7).; Delight to know his ways and to draw near (v2) can stand beside oppression in the same people.

19641.text: Jeremiah 33:24: "'The Lord has rejected the two clans that he chose'? Thus they have despised my people": *"Have you not observed that these people are saying, 'The Lord has rejected the two clans that he chose'? Thus they have despised my people so that they are no longer a nation in their sight"* (v24).; Others look at the state of the chosen and draw a conclusion about God: he has rejected them. Their contempt rests on that conclusion. "Despised" is *nāʾaṣ* (*to spurn*; H5006). The measure is their own: *"in their sight"*. "Rejected" is *māʾas* (H3988A), the same verb as *"refuse the evil"* in Isaiah 7:15 (§2a).; God answers with the fixed order of creation: *"If I have not established my covenant with day and night and the fixed order of heaven and earth, then I will reject the offspring of Jacob and David my servant and will not choose one of his offspring to rule"* (v25–26). It ends: *"For I will restore their fortunes and will have mercy on them"* (v26).

19642.text: What others do around a choice, in these verses: grumble against the chosen man, and God counts it as against himself (Num 16:11; 17:5, 10); seek more than they were given, and are jealous (Num 16:10; Psa 106:16); name a choice as shame, and are angry at what it costs them (1Sa 20:30–31); despise the chosen in the heart, by the eyes of people (2Sa 6:16, 20); despise and abhor the chosen servant (Isa 49:7); conclude from the chosen people's ruin that God rejected them, and despise them in their own sight (Jer 33:24); ask to share the joy of the chosen (Psa 106:5); not know God, and still be called and equipped for the sake of the chosen (Isa 45:4–5); offer an inner act, the humbling of the soul, that God's choosing weighs and does not accept (Isa 58:3–5)

19643.text: Whose measure. It comes up in four verses. Michal measures by *"the eyes of his servants' female servants"* (2Sa 6:20). The people in Jer 33:24 measure *"in their sight"*. Over against both, David celebrates *"before the Lord"* (2Sa 6:21), and Isa 49:7 gives the Lord's faithfulness and choosing. The same theme is in batch 1 (Deu 12:8) and in §2a ("whose measure").

19644.text: What God does in reply. In Num 17:5 he makes the choice plain. In Isa 49:7 he promises that kings will bow. In Jer 33:25–26 he points to the fixed order of day and night. Under rule 72 these acts are God's and go to Ch 13. They are recorded here because each one answers what the others did.

19645.text: The same word in two verses. Michal's *"despised"* (2Sa 6:16) and the servant *"deeply despised"* (Isa 49:7) are the same verb, *bāzâ* (H0959). The verses are side by side. The text does not join them.

19646.text: Not about choosing: Judg 20:34 and Pro 10:20. Each has an inner-being note for another section (knowing and fear; speaking), noted and not placed.

19647.text: Already read: Isa 7:16 and Isa 66:3, in §2a.

19648.text: Corrections to the HIB/qualifier file: Isa 66:3, the soul is the chooser's own (§2a, "paired"), not "other".

19650.text: OT-62. Two of its seven verses are read here (1Sa 20:30, Psa 106:23). The other five are outside the choose set. OT-62 stays open for them.

19651.text: Isaiah 7:15–16 — "when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good": The setting is a king’s heart in fear. Syria and Ephraim are marching on Jerusalem, and *"the heart of Ahaz and the heart of his people shook as the trees of the forest shake before the wind"* (v2). The Lord sends Isaiah with a word for that heart: *"Be careful, be quiet, do not fear, and do not let your heart be faint"* (v4); the threat *"shall not stand"* (v7); then the condition: *"If you are not firm in faith, you will not be firm at all"* (v9). Both "firm" words are the one verb (H0539), so standing firm and being kept firm are the same word.; Then the Lord makes Ahaz an offer: *"Ask a sign of the Lord your God; let it be deep as Sheol or high as heaven"* (v11). Ahaz refuses, in pious words: *"I will not ask, and I will not put the Lord to the test"* (v12). The answer shows what that refusal was: *"Is it too little for you to weary men, that you weary my God also?"* (v13). Ahaz’s refusal was a choice. He chose not to take hold of what the Lord held out.; The sign is given anyway, and at its centre is a child who has what Ahaz lacked: *"He shall eat curds and honey when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"* (v15). The act is one act with two sides: refusing the evil (H3988A); choosing the good (H0977); Refusing is not a step before the choice. It is the choice seen from the other side. Both rest on a knowing: *"when he knows how"*. The verse marks the moment a person can tell evil from good and turn from the one to the other.; The verse ties the eating to that knowing: he eats *"when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"*. The oracle itself says what curds and honey are. *"In that day … because of the abundance of milk that they give, he will eat curds, for everyone who is left in the land will eat curds and honey"* (v21–22). It is the food of those left in the land after the Lord has swept it with *"the king of Assyria"*: vineyards turned to *"briers and thorns"*, hills *"where cattle are let loose"* (v23–25). The child who refuses the evil and chooses the good eats with those who are left, and eats from abundance, in a land stripped of what it had.

19652.text: Isaiah 7:15–16 — "when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good": The next verse sets a second consequence against the same knowing: *"before the boy knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good, the land whose two kings you dread will be deserted"* (v16). What Ahaz feared will be gone. Then comes what Ahaz’s own choice brings on him: *"The Lord will bring upon you and upon your people and upon your father’s house such days as have not come … the king of Assyria!"* (v17).; The oracle uses the same verb for refusing once more. Isaiah 8:6 has *"Because this people has refused the waters of Shiloah that flow gently"*, and it is the same word as *"refuse the evil"* (H3988A). Its consequence is the opposite of a gentle stream: *"the waters of the River, mighty and many, the king of Assyria"* overflowing *"even to the neck"*, and filling *"the breadth of your land, O Immanuel"* (8:7–8).; So in one oracle refusing runs both ways: the child refuses the evil and chooses the good, and eats among those who are left; Ahaz refuses the sign, and the people refuse the gentle waters, and the flood comes; I read the passage as setting the right refusing against the wrong refusing, each with its consequence. The text does not join them in one sentence; it places them in one oracle.

19655.text: Isaiah 66:3–4 — "These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations": The oracle opens with the Lord’s greatness and with the person he looks to: *"Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool; what is the house that you would build for me"* (v1); *"But this is the one to whom I will look: he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word"* (v2); Before any choosing is described, the oracle has set out the inner being the Lord looks for: humbled, contrite, trembling at his word.; Against that stands worship that looks right and is not: *"He who slaughters an ox is like one who kills a man; he who sacrifices a lamb, like one who breaks a dog’s neck"* … *"like one who blesses an idol"* (v3). The outward act is the same as before; what has gone wrong is inside. The verse says where: *"These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations."* Choosing and the soul’s delight stand side by side. They chose their own ways, and their soul (H5315) takes pleasure in what the Lord calls abominations.; The word for delight is the same on both sides: their soul *"delights"* in abominations (v3); they *"chose that in which I did not delight"* (v4); Both are H2654A. So the choosing comes down to whose delight governs it: the soul’s own, or the Lord's.; The Lord’s answer is a choice of his own, in the same verb: *"I also will choose harsh treatment for them and bring their fears upon them"* (v4). What he brings is *their fears* (H4035): what they themselves dreaded. Set against v2 and v5, the contrast is in the inner being. The one who *"trembles at my word"* is looked on. Those who chose their own ways are given what they feared.; The reason is given in the same words as 65:12: *"because when I called, no one answered, when I spoke, they did not listen; but they did what was evil in my eyes and chose that in which I did not delight"* (v4). Their choosing is the end of not answering and not listening.; The oracle carries on to those around the choosers: The ones who chose their own ways turn on those who tremble: *"Your brothers who hate you and cast you out for my name’s sake"*, and mock them with *"Let the Lord be glorified, that we may see your joy"*. The verdict is *"it is they who shall be put to shame"* (v5).

19657.text: Refusing is choosing (Isa 7:15–16). The act is one act with two sides, and refusing can go either way. The child refuses the evil. Ahaz refuses the sign, and the people refuse the gentle waters (8:6), with the same verb. This sharpens the test reading of Isa 65:12, which said that not answering and not listening are already choosing: in Isa 8:6 the refusal is named outright.

19658.text: Choosing rests on knowing how (Isa 7:15). It is a knowing *how* to tell evil from good and turn. In Isa 1 the oracle opens with its absence: *"Israel does not know, my people do not understand"* (1:3).

19659.text: Choosing goes with desire and delight. It is paired with *"desired"* (1:29) and with the soul’s delight (66:3). In Isa 66 the delight word is the same on both sides, so the choice is a question of whose delight governs it.

19660.text: The choice is laid out as an offer, with both outcomes (Isa 1:16–20). *"cease to do evil, learn to do good"*; *"willing"* or *"refuse"*; eat, or be eaten. In Isa 7:15 the right choice also ends in eating.

19661.text: What is chosen comes back on the chooser. Each of these is stated in its verse: *"Destiny"* and *"destine"* (65:11–12, from the test); the chosen gardens and oaks become the image of the chooser withering (1:29–30); the strong man’s own work becomes the spark (1:31); *"I also will choose … their fears"* (66:4); I read these as the same move in different figures. Each verse makes it on its own.

19664.text: Psalm 25:12 — "Him will he instruct in the way that he should choose": The psalm is a prayer from someone in trouble. It begins *"To you, O Lord, I lift up my soul"*; *"O my God, in you I trust; let me not be put to shame"* (v1–2). It ends with that same person *"lonely and afflicted"*. Among the trouble: *"The troubles of my heart are enlarged"* (v17); *"how many are my foes, and with what violent hatred they hate me"* (v19); *"guard my soul … Let me not be put to shame"* (v20); Running through the whole psalm is the person's own guilt: *"Remember not the sins of my youth or my transgressions"* (v7); *"pardon my guilt, for it is great"* (v11); *"forgive all my sins"* (v18); The person who asks about the way is a sinner, and says so.; Before the verse about choosing, the psalmist asks for the way three times over: *"Make me to know your ways, O Lord; teach me your paths"* (v4); *"Lead me in your truth and teach me"* (v5); Then he says why he can expect it, from who the Lord is: *"Good and upright is the Lord; therefore he instructs sinners in the way. He leads the humble in what is right, and teaches the humble his way"* (v8–9). The Lord's instructing comes out of his goodness. It is given to sinners and to the humble.; Then comes the verse: *"Who is the man who fears the Lord? Him will he instruct in the way that he should choose"* (v12). The word "instruct" is the same in v8 and v12 (H3384B). The person who chooses here does not make up the way. The way to choose is taught, and the one who is taught it is the one who fears the Lord. The fear comes first, then the teaching, then the choice. The verse does not say the man chooses well on his own; it says the Lord instructs him in what he should choose.; What follows the choice is stated: *"His soul shall abide in well-being, and his offspring shall inherit the land"* (v13). "Well-being" here (H2896B) is the same word as *"the good"* in Isaiah 7:15, *"refuse the evil and choose the good"*. The man taught the way he should choose has his soul *"abide"*, lodge or stay, in the good.; *"The friendship of the Lord is for those who fear him, and he makes known to them his covenant"* (v14). The teaching goes further than a direction to take. The one who fears the Lord is brought into his friendship, and the covenant is made known (H3045, "know", as in v4).

19665.text: Psalm 25:12 — "Him will he instruct in the way that he should choose": The psalmist then turns his eyes: *"My eyes are ever toward the Lord, for he will pluck my feet out of the net"* (v15). Where the eyes are turned decides where the feet are kept from.; The heart's trouble comes back after the choosing verse, not before it. *"The troubles of my heart are enlarged"* (v17) uses the same verb as Psalm 119:32, *"when you enlarge my heart"* (H7337). In Psalm 25 it is the troubles that widen in the heart. In Psalm 119 it is the heart that the Lord widens so the chooser can run. I note the shared word; neither psalm refers to the other.; The psalm does not end with a person who has chosen and is now safe. It ends with waiting: *"May integrity and uprightness preserve me, for I wait for you"* (v21). The way chosen is held while waiting on the Lord, with the troubles still there.

19666.text: Isaiah 56:4 — "who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant": The oracle opens with a command and a reason: *"Keep justice, and do righteousness, for soon my salvation will come, and my righteousness be revealed"* (v1). Then a blessing on the one who *"holds it fast, who keeps the Sabbath, not profaning it, and keeps his hand from doing any evil"* (v2). The holding fast and the keeping from evil are already there before the choosing verse.; The verse is addressed to two people who speak about themselves: *"Let not the foreigner who has joined himself to the Lord say"*, *"The Lord will surely separate me from his people"*; *"let not the eunuch say"*, *"Behold, I am a dry tree"* (v3); Each one has a judgement about himself: shut out, and fruitless. The foreigner expects to be separated. The eunuch sees himself as a tree with no sap and no fruit, with no sons and daughters to carry his name. The Lord tells them both not to say it.; Then he describes the eunuchs he means: *"who keep my Sabbaths, who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant"* (v4). The word "please" is H2654A, the same word as *"delight"* in Isaiah 65:12 and 66:4 (*"chose what I did not delight in"*, *"chose that in which I did not delight"*). Here the choosing goes the other way. These choose what the Lord delights in. The measure is the same as in those two oracles, the Lord's delight, and here it is met.; The choosing stands between keeping and holding fast: *"keep my Sabbaths"*; *"choose the things that please me"*; *"hold fast my covenant"* (H2388H, the same word as *"holds it fast"* in v2); The choice is not one moment. It sits inside a keeping and a holding on.; The Lord's answer goes straight to what the eunuch said about himself: *"I will give in my house and within my walls a monument and a name better than sons and daughters; I will give them an everlasting name that shall not be cut off"* (v5). The man who called himself a dry tree is given a name that outlasts children. The foreigner who feared being separated is brought in: *"these I will bring to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer; their burnt offerings and their sacrifices will be accepted"* (v7).

19667.text: Isaiah 56:4 — "who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant": The foreigners are described in inner terms as well: they *"join themselves to the Lord, to minister to him, to love the name of the Lord, and to be his servants"* (v6). Love of the name stands with the keeping and the holding fast.; What follows in the chapter is the opposite. Israel's own watchmen *"are all without knowledge"*. They are *"shepherds who have no understanding; they have all turned to their own way, each to his own gain"* (v10–11). "Their own way" is the same phrase as in Isaiah 66:3, *"These have chosen their own ways"* (H1870G). The outsiders who choose what the Lord delights in are brought in. The insiders turn to their own way.

19668.text: What this verse shows of choosing: Choosing what the Lord delights in is the positive counterpart to choosing what he does not delight in (65:12, 66:4). The measure is the same.; The choice is held inside keeping and holding fast. It is not a single act.; It is made by people whose own judgement of themselves is "shut out" and "a dry tree", and the Lord answers that judgement directly.; The outcome is a name that is not cut off, a place in his house, joy in prayer, and acceptance.; The love of his name goes with it.; Its opposite in the same chapter is turning to one's own way, by those who should know and do not.

19669.text: The way to choose is taught (Psa 25:8, 12). The Lord instructs sinners and the humble out of his goodness, and the one who fears him is taught *"the way that he should choose"*. This stands beside Psalm 119:29, where the psalmist asks God to put the false way far off. In both psalms the chooser does not stand alone.

19670.text: Fear of the Lord comes before the choosing (Psa 25:12, 14). The test reading of Joshua 24 had *"fear the Lord and serve him"* (v14) before the choice. Psalm 25 puts the fear first explicitly: it is the man who fears whom the Lord instructs.

19671.text: The good chosen is the good the soul lives in. Isaiah 7:15 has *"choose the good"*, and Psalm 25:13 has *"His soul shall abide in well-being"*. It is the same word (H2896B). I read this as the good that is chosen becoming the place where the soul lives. Each verse says its own half; neither refers to the other.

19672.text: Choosing what the Lord delights in (Isa 56:4). This is the counterpart to Isaiah 65:12 and 66:4. With the three verses together, "the things that please me" and "what I did not delight in" are the two sides of one measure.

19673.text: The choice is held, not just made. It is set between keeping and holding fast (Isa 56:2, 4, 6), and between eyes turned to the Lord and waiting (Psa 25:15, 21). This sits with the test readings: the heart inclined after the choice (Jos 24:23), and clinging to the testimonies (Psa 119:31).

19677.text: For the next batches: batch 3 is people choosing of their own accord, and choosing together (Deu 23:16, 2Sa 19:38, 2Cor 8:17, Act 6:5, Act 15:22 and 25), with the wisdom sayings Pro 3:31 and 16:16. These are mostly not choices between God and other gods. Whether they show the same tie to what the eyes see, to delight and to knowing is to be read from them.

19678.text: Deuteronomy 23:16 — "in the place that he shall choose … wherever it suits him": The law concerns *"a slave who has escaped from his master to you"*. Israel is told *"You shall not give up to his master"* (v15). Then the choice is handed to the slave: *"He shall dwell with you, in your midst, in the place that he shall choose within one of your towns, wherever it suits him. You shall not wrong him"* (v16).; The man who escaped had no say over where he lived. The law gives it back to him. The choice is his, and its ground is his own good: *"wherever it suits him"* is literally "in what is good to him" (H2896A). Israel's part is to honour it: not to hand him back, and not to *"wrong him"* (H3238, to oppress).; The phrase is a weighty one in Deuteronomy. *"the place that he shall choose within one of your towns"* has the same shape as the phrase Deuteronomy uses for the Lord’s own choosing: *"the place that the Lord your God will choose out of all your tribes"* (12:5); *"the place that the Lord will choose in one of your tribes"* (12:14). The words (place, that, choose, in one of your …) are the same (H4725, H0977). I read this as the law giving the escaped slave, in his own small measure, the kind of choosing the Lord keeps for his own dwelling. The verse does not draw the comparison.

19679.text: 2 Samuel 19:38 — "whatever seems good to you, and all that you desire of me": Barzillai had fed David in his flight. He came with others bringing *"honey and curds and sheep and cheese from the herd, for David and the people with him to eat"*, saying *"The people are hungry and weary and thirsty in the wilderness"* (17:27, 29). When David returns, the king offers him a place at court: *"Come over with me, and I will provide for you with me in Jerusalem"* (19:33).; Barzillai declines, and his reason is about his own inner capacity: *"I am this day eighty years old. Can I discern what is pleasant and what is not? Can your servant taste what he eats or what he drinks? Can I still listen to the voice of singing men and singing women?"* (v35). The Hebrew is "know between good and evil" (H3045 with H0996, H2896B, H7451A). It is the same pairing as Isaiah 7:15–16, *"knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"*. Here it is the knowing of taste and pleasure, and Barzillai says that at eighty it has gone. The same words, put to the palate rather than to right and wrong, mark a change of face (#1919).; He makes his choice, and it is for someone else: *"Please let your servant return, that I may die in my own city … But here is your servant Chimham. Let him go over with my lord the king, and do for him whatever seems good to you"* (v37).; The king hands the choosing back to Barzillai: *"Chimham shall go over with me, and I will do for him whatever seems good to you, and all that you desire of me I will do for you"* (v38). *"Whatever seems good to you"* is literally "the good in your eyes" (H2896A, H5869). *"all that you desire of me"* is the choosing verb (H0977): "all that you choose of me". So the old man who says he can no longer tell good from bad on his palate is given the king's word that what is good in his eyes will be done.; The outcome is told: *"the king kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and he returned to his own home"* (v39); *"Chimham went on with him"* (v40).

19682.text: Acts 6:5 — "what they said pleased the whole gathering, and they chose Stephen": The choice is made at a point of division: *"a complaint by the Hellenists arose against the Hebrews because their widows were being neglected in the daily distribution"* (v1). The twelve do not choose. They give the gathering the choice and the measure for it: *"pick out from among you seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom"* (v3).; The gathering's response is inward before it is an act: *"what they said pleased the whole gathering"* (G0700). Then *"they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit"*, and six others (v5). The choosing comes from the whole gathering being pleased, and it follows the measure they were given: the men are known for what is in them (Spirit, wisdom, faith), not for rank.; The outcome: *"These they set before the apostles, and they prayed and laid their hands on them"* (v6). The narrative goes straight on: *"the word of God continued to increase, and the number of the disciples multiplied greatly"* (v7). It places the increase next to the choosing; it does not say one caused the other.

19683.text: Acts 15:22, 25 — "it seemed good … having come to one accord, to choose men": The choosing ends a dispute that went to the heart of the faith. Some taught *"Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved"* (v1), and there was *"no small dissension and debate"* (v2).; At the council the first word about choosing is God's. Peter says *"Brothers, you know that in the early days God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe"* (v7). It is the same verb as the church's later choosing (G1586). He goes on: *"God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them, by giving them the Holy Spirit … having cleansed their hearts by faith"* (v8–9). The assembly *"fell silent"* and *"listened"* (v12). James gives his judgement from the prophets (v13–21).; Then the church chooses: *"it seemed good to the apostles and the elders, with the whole church, to choose men from among them and send them to Antioch"* (v22). The letter says how they came to it: *"it has seemed good to us, having come to one accord, to choose men and send them to you"* (v25). "One accord" (G3661) is a single shared mind. The same verb for "seemed good" (G1380) then joins them to the Spirit: *"it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us"* (v28).; So the church's choosing: follows God's choosing, in the same verb; follows listening in silence; comes from one accord; is joined to what seemed good to the Holy Spirit; The outcome is in the hearers' hearts: *"when they had read it, they rejoiced because of its encouragement"* (v31). Judas and Silas *"encouraged and strengthened the brothers"* (v32), and were *"sent off in peace"* (v33). The letter answers the *"unsettling"* of their *"minds"* (v24).

19687.text: Choosing as a person's own freedom, honoured. In Deu 23:16 and 2Sa 19:38 the ground is the chooser's own good: *"wherever it suits him"*, *"whatever seems good to you"*. Others are bound to honour it. This is a face not seen in batches 1–2, where the choosing was between the Lord and something else. Here "good in your eyes" is honoured. In Jos 24:15, "evil in your eyes" was where the choice against the Lord could start. The same expression changes character with the setting (#1919).

19689.text: Choosing together. The church chooses out of a shared inward response (*"pleased the whole gathering"*) and in *"one accord"*. Its choosing follows God's own choosing, uses the same verb, and is joined to what *"seemed good to the Holy Spirit"* (Act 6:5; 15:7, 22, 25, 28). The outcome is in hearts: joy, encouragement, peace.

19690.text: The pull before the choice. *"Do not envy … and do not choose"* (Pro 3:31): the command reaches the envy as well as the choice. This stands beside batch 1, where *"desired"* is paired with *"chosen"* (Isa 1:29) and the soul's delight with choosing one's own ways (Isa 66:3).

19691.text: Choosing as preferring. *"to be chosen rather than silver"* (Pro 16:16): to choose is to weigh and set above. What is to be preferred is inward, and it is valued above *"nothing you desire"* (Pro 3:15).

19692.text: The knowing of good and evil has more than one face. In Isa 7:15 it is the knowing that grounds choosing the good. In 2Sa 19:35 the same words are the palate's knowing of pleasant and unpleasant, and they fade with age.

19694.text: Kept open: Deu 23:16 echoes the phrase used for the place the Lord chooses (Deu 12). I have marked this "I read". Whether it is to be read as more than a shared form of words is for the researcher.

19695.text: For the next batch: batch 4 is the Job verses (Job 15:5, 34:4, 34:33, 36:21). These are read as choices weighed by another party, per the researcher's F1 ruling, and kept in their own section.

19696.text: 232 verses, 243 rows. Eleven verses carry two hits: 2Sa 10:9 and 1Ch 19:10: "chose … the best"; 1Ki 8:16, 2Ch 6:5 and 2Ch 6:6: a city and a man; 1Ch 28:4: "me" and "Judah"; 2Ch 13:3: both armies; Isa 66:4: God's choosing and theirs; Mar 13:20: "the elect, whom he chose"; Joh 15:16: "You did not choose me, but I chose you"; 1Cor 1:27: "God chose … God chose"; None of the five new words shares a verse with the first five.

19699.text: 3.1 God chooses: a place, so that his name dwells there (44): The phrase repeats through Deuteronomy: "the place that the Lord your God will choose, to make his name dwell there" (Deu 12:11; also 14:23, 16:2, 16:6, 16:11, 26:2).

19700.text: Kings and Chronicles narrow it: from "I chose no city out of all the tribes of Israel" (1Ki 8:16, 2Ch 6:5); to "I have chosen Jerusalem that my name may be there" (2Ch 6:6)

19701.text: The choice carries God's own presence and attention: "For now I have chosen and consecrated this house that my name may be there forever. My eyes and my heart will be there for all time" (2Ch 7:16).

19702.text: People's acts are directed to the chosen place: worship, eating, rejoicing: "you shall rejoice before the Lord your God … at the place that the Lord your God will choose" (Deu 16:11); judgement: Deu 17:8, 17:10; reading the law: Deu 31:11; prayer in repentance: "if they repent with all their heart and with all their soul … and pray to you toward … the city that you have chosen" (1Ki 8:48; 2Ch 6:38)

19703.text: Learning is stated as a purpose: "that you may learn to fear the Lord your God always" (Deu 14:23).

19704.text: The chosen city can be cast off, and chosen again: "I will cast off this city that I have chosen, Jerusalem" (2Ki 23:27); "the Lord will again comfort Zion and again choose Jerusalem" (Zec 1:17; also Zec 2:12); The choice is named against an accuser: "The Lord who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you!" (Zec 3:2)

19705.text: The verses give love as the ground, and deny number as the ground: "because he loved your fathers and chose their offspring after them" (Deu 4:37); "It was not because you were more in number … that the Lord set his love on you and chose you, for you were the fewest of all peoples" (Deu 7:7); "the Lord set his heart in love on your fathers and chose their offspring" (Deu 10:15); "Mount Zion, which he loves" (Psa 78:68); "the pride of Jacob whom he loves" (Psa 47:4)

19706.text: What the choosing makes them: "a people for his treasured possession" (Deu 7:6, 14:2); "his heritage" (Psa 33:12); "his own possession" (Psa 135:4)

19707.text: "Chosen" becomes their name (H0972): "O offspring of Israel his servant, children of Jacob, his chosen ones!" (1Ch 16:13; Psa 105:6); "So he brought his people out with joy, his chosen ones with singing" (Psa 105:43); "that I may look upon the prosperity of your chosen ones, that I may rejoice in the gladness of your nation" (Psa 106:5); "to give drink to my chosen people" (Isa 43:20)

19708.text: Purpose: "my servant whom I have chosen, that you may know and believe me and understand that I am he" (Isa 43:10); Cyrus is called "For the sake of my servant Jacob, and Israel my chosen … though you do not know me" (Isa 45:4).

19709.text: What the chosen will have: "my chosen shall possess it, and my servants shall dwell there" (Isa 65:9); "my chosen shall long enjoy the work of their hands" (Isa 65:22); against those who "shall leave your name to my chosen for a curse" (Isa 65:15)

19710.text: The verses pair the choosing with not casting off, with comfort, and with help: "I have chosen you and not cast you off" (Isa 41:9); "Fear not, O Jacob my servant, Jeshurun whom I have chosen" (Isa 44:2); "the Lord will have compassion on Jacob and will again choose Israel" (Isa 14:1)

19711.text: Rejection stands beside choosing: "He rejected the tent of Joseph; he did not choose the tribe of Ephraim, but he chose the tribe of Judah" (Psa 78:67–68); Others can say the choice has been withdrawn: "The Lord has rejected the two clans that he chose" (Jer 33:24).

19712.text: God's choosing is linked to his oath: "On the day when I chose Israel, I swore to the offspring of the house of Jacob" (Eze 20:5).

19713.text: Retold in the NT: "The God of this people Israel chose our fathers and made the people great" (Act 13:17).

19714.text: Its ground, as the verses state it: "chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him" (Eph 1:4); "in order that God's purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of him who calls" (Rom 9:11; said of the twins "not yet born"); "a remnant, chosen by grace" (Rom 11:5); "brothers loved by God, that he has chosen you" (1Th 1:4); "God chose you as the firstfruits to be saved, through sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth" (2Th 2:13, G0138)

19715.text: What it makes them: "a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession, that you may proclaim the excellencies of him who called you" (1Pe 2:9). This is near the wording of Deu 7:6.; "Put on then, as God's chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience" (Col 3:12). Being chosen is followed by what to put on.

19716.text: Called and chosen are not the same: "For many are called, but few are chosen" (Mat 22:14); "those with him are called and chosen and faithful" (Rev 17:14); The person's part: "be all the more diligent to confirm your calling and election, for if you practice these qualities you will never fall" (2Pe 1:10).

19717.text: God's care for the elect: "for the sake of the elect, whom he chose, he shortened the days" (Mar 13:20; Mat 24:22); The elect are a target: false christs arise "to lead astray, if possible, even the elect" (Mat 24:24; Mar 13:22).; The elect are gathered: "they will gather his elect from the four winds" (Mat 24:31; Mar 13:27).; "will not God give justice to his elect, who cry to him day and night?" (Luk 18:7); "Who shall bring any charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies" (Rom 8:33)

19720.text: Persons named so: "Rufus, chosen in the Lord" (Rom 16:13); "the elect lady" (2Jo 1) and "your elect sister" (2Jo 13); "the elect angels" (1Ti 5:21)

19721.text: 3.4 God chooses the foolish, weak, low and poor (3): "God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise; God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong" (1Cor 1:27); "God chose what is low and despised in the world, even things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are" (1Cor 1:28); "has not God chosen those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom, which he has promised to those who love him?" (Jam 2:5); The verses give purposes: "to shame", "to bring to nothing", "to be rich in faith".; This stands beside "not because you were more in number" (Deu 7:7, §3.2).

19722.text: Priesthood and Levites: "the Lord your God has chosen him … to stand and minister in the name of the Lord" (Deu 18:5); also Deu 21:5, 1Ch 15:2, 2Ch 29:11; Choosing goes with bringing near: "The one whom he chooses he will bring near to him" (Num 16:5); "Blessed is the one you choose and bring near, to dwell in your courts!" (Psa 65:4).; The choice is shown, not argued: "the staff of the man whom I choose shall sprout" (Num 17:5).

19723.text: King: "a king over you whom the Lord your God will choose" (Deu 17:15); Samuel's sons of Jesse are passed over one by one: "Neither has the Lord chosen this one" (1Sa 16:8, 16:9, 16:10). 19727.text: The Son: from the cloud: "This is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him!" (Luk 9:35); mocked at the cross: "let him save himself, if he is the Christ of God, his Chosen One!" (Luk 23:35); "a living stone rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen and precious" (1Pe 2:4); "a cornerstone chosen and precious, and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame" (1Pe 2:6); Chosen by God and rejected by men are stated together.

In Philippians the choice is held open, with no answer given.

19835.text: H0977, "choose". This is the ordinary verb, and it carries most of these verses. The ESV renders it in several ways: *"choose"*; *"desire"*: *"all that you desire of me I will do for you"* (2Sa 19:38); *"to be chosen"* in the sense of preferred: *"To get understanding is to be chosen rather than silver"* (Pro 16:16); The same verb is used of the Lord choosing the place for his name (Deu 12:5, 14), and of the Lord's answering choice: *"I also will choose harsh treatment for them"* (Isa 66:4).

19836.text: H3988A, "refuse, reject, despise". This is the other side of the act: *"refuse the evil"* (Isa 7:15); *"this people has refused the waters of Shiloah"* (Isa 8:6); *"because you reject it"* (Job 34:33); Job's last word: *"I despise myself, and repent"* (Job 42:6)

19837.text: G1586, "choose" (Greek). Used for the gathering choosing the seven (Act 6:5), for the church choosing men to send (Act 15:22, 25), and for God's own choice before them: *"God made a choice among you"* (Act 15:7).

19839.text: Choosing has two sides: Refusing is itself choosing. The child *"knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"* (Isa 7:15). The oracle around that verse shows refusing going both ways. Ahaz refuses the Lord's offer of a sign with pious words: *"I will not ask, and I will not put the Lord to the test"* (Isa 7:12). The people *"refused the waters of Shiloah that flow gently"* (8:6). The right refusing and the wrong refusing are set in one oracle, each with its own consequence.; Not answering is already choosing. *"when I called, you did not answer; when I spoke, you did not listen, but you did what was evil in my eyes and chose what I did not delight in"* (Isa 65:12; repeated in 66:4). The choosing of what the Lord does not delight in is where the not-listening ends up.; The choice is laid out with both its sides and both its ends: *"cease to do evil, learn to do good"*; *"If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land"*; *"but if you refuse and rebel, you shall be eaten by the sword"* (Isa 1:16–20).

19840.text: Knowing how. The child chooses *"when he knows how"* (Isa 7:15). The oracle of Isaiah 1 opens with the absence of that knowing: *"Israel does not know, my people do not understand"* (1:3).

19841.text: Being taught. *"Who is the man who fears the Lord? Him will he instruct in the way that he should choose"* (Psa 25:12). The teaching comes from who the Lord is: *"Good and upright is the Lord; therefore he instructs sinners in the way"* (25:8). The psalmist asks for it: *"Make me to know your ways, O Lord; teach me your paths"* (25:4). In Psalm 119 he asks *"graciously teach me your law"*, and asks God to do the refusing with him: *"Put false ways far from me"* (119:29).

19842.text: The fear of the Lord. In Psalm 25 the fear comes first, then the teaching, then the choice (25:12). Joshua puts the same order before the people: *"fear the Lord and serve him in sincerity and in faithfulness"* (Jos 24:14), and then *"choose this day"*.

19844.text: What is good to the chooser. Two verses make the chooser's own good the ground, and honour it: *"wherever it suits him"* (Deu 23:16) and *"whatever seems good to you"* (2Sa 19:38). In Hebrew both say "the good" to him, or in his eyes.

19845.text: Desire and delight. Choosing comes paired with desire: *"the oaks that you desired … the gardens that you have chosen"* (Isa 1:29). It comes with the soul's delight: *"These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations"* (Isa 66:3).

19846.text: Envy. The pull can be named before the choice, and the command reaches it: *"Do not envy a man of violence and do not choose any of his ways"* (Pro 3:31).

19847.text: Being pleased, and earnestness. In the church at Jerusalem the choosing comes out of a shared inward response: *"what they said pleased the whole gathering, and they chose"* (Act 6:5). Titus goes *"being himself very earnest … of his own accord"* (2Cor 8:17).

19848.text: Preferring. To choose can be to weigh one good against another and set it above: *"How much better to get wisdom than gold! To get understanding is to be chosen rather than silver"* (Pro 16:16). Proverbs 3 sets the weighing against all desire: *"nothing you desire can compare with her"* (3:15).

19849.text: The chooser's eyes. *"if it is evil in your eyes to serve the Lord, choose this day"* (Jos 24:15). Here the chooser's own sight is where turning from the Lord could begin.

19850.text: The Lord's eyes. *"you did what was evil in my eyes"* (Isa 65:12). The measure is the Lord's sight.

19851.text: The Lord's delight, failed. *"chose what I did not delight in"* (Isa 65:12); *"chose that in which I did not delight"* (66:4).

19852.text: The Lord's delight, met. *"who choose the things that please me"* (Isa 56:4). It is the same word, so the three verses are the two sides of one measure.

19853.text: The soul's own delight, set against the Lord's. *"their soul delights in their abominations"* (Isa 66:3). The word is the same one again.

19855.text: Choosing before a God who has already acted: In these verses the human choice is never the first move.; At Shechem it comes after eleven verses of what the Lord did, beginning with *"I took your father Abraham from beyond the River"* (Jos 24:3).; In Isaiah 65 the wrong choice is made in front of a God who says *"Here I am, here I am"* and *"I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people"* (65:1–2).; At the Jerusalem council the church's choosing follows Peter's word that *"God made a choice among you"* (Act 15:7), in the same verb.

19857.text: Choosing together: A people can choose as one.; Israel at Shechem: *"we will serve the Lord"*, and they become *"witnesses against yourselves"* (Jos 24:21–22).; The gathering in Jerusalem, out of being pleased (Act 6:5).; The church, *"having come to one accord"* (Act 15:25).; Weighing a case together is also called choosing: *"Let us choose what is right; let us know among ourselves what is good"* (Job 34:4).

19858.text: A choice that is honoured: Choosing is a freedom a person can lose, and Scripture gives it back. The escaped slave *"shall dwell with you … in the place that he shall choose within one of your towns, wherever it suits him. You shall not wrong him"* (Deu 23:16). The king hands the choice to the man who fed him in the wilderness: *"all that you desire of me I will do for you"* (2Sa 19:38).; The phrase *"the place that he shall choose within one of your towns"* has the same wording as *"the place that the Lord your God will choose"* (Deu 12:5, 14). I read this as the law giving the slave a small share of the kind of choosing the Lord keeps for his own dwelling. The verse does not draw this comparison (open item).

19859.text: It binds. *"You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen the Lord"* (Jos 24:22).

19862.text: It is held by keeping in view and clinging. *"I have chosen the way of faithfulness; I set your rules before me. I cling to your testimonies"* (Psa 119:30–31). The verb for "cling" is the one used two verses earlier: *"My soul clings to the dust"* (119:25). What the soul clings to has turned.

19863.text: It is held by keeping and holding fast. *"who keep my Sabbaths, who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant"* (Isa 56:4).

19871.text: affliction, as Elihu reads it: *"this you have chosen rather than affliction"* (Job 36:21)

19872.text: When the choice is right, the outcome reaches the inner being: *"His soul shall abide in well-being"* (Psa 25:13). "Well-being" is the same word as *"the good"* in *"choose the good"* (Isa 7:15). I read this as the good that is chosen becoming the place the soul lives.; *"The friendship of the Lord is for those who fear him"* (Psa 25:14). The upright are *"in his confidence"* (Pro 3:32), which is the same word.; *"I will … make them joyful in my house of prayer"* (Isa 56:7).; *"they rejoiced because of its encouragement"*, and Judas and Silas were *"sent off in peace"* (Act 15:31, 33).; Barzillai: *"the king kissed Barzillai and blessed him"* (2Sa 19:39).; The child who refuses the evil and chooses the good eats *"curds and honey"*, the food of *"everyone who is left in the land"* (Isa 7:15, 22). In the other oracle, *"If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land"* (Isa 1:19).

19873.text: Shame at the thing chosen: *"they shall be ashamed of the oaks that you desired; and you shall blush for the gardens that you have chosen"* (Isa 1:29); *"you shall be put to shame"* (Isa 65:13); *"it is they who shall be put to shame"* (Isa 66:5).

19875.text: Their own fears: *"I also will choose harsh treatment for them and bring their fears upon them"* (Isa 66:4).

19876.text: What is chosen comes back on the chooser. Each of these is stated in its own verse: They set *"cups of mixed wine for Destiny"*, and the Lord says *"I will destine you to the sword"*. "Destiny" and "destine" share a root (Isa 65:11–12).; They chose gardens and desired oaks, and become *"like an oak whose leaf withers, and like a garden without water"* (Isa 1:30).; *"the strong shall become tinder, and his work a spark"* (Isa 1:31).; The Lord's choice answers theirs: *"I also will choose"* (Isa 66:4).; I read these as the same thing said in different figures.

19878.text: They read the choice from the words. Eliphaz: *"your iniquity teaches your mouth, and you choose the tongue of the crafty. Your own mouth condemns you"* (Job 15:5–6). He goes from the mouth to the heart: *"Why does your heart carry you away, and why do your eyes flash"* (15:12).

19879.text: They weigh it as tasting. Elihu: *"the ear tests words as the palate tastes food"*; *"Let us choose what is right"* (Job 34:3–4).

19880.text: They read it in suffering. Elihu: *"this you have chosen rather than affliction"*, seen in wrath and scoffing (Job 36:18, 21).

19881.text: They cannot make the choice for the other. *"For you must choose, and not I"* (Job 34:33).

19883.text: "Good / evil in your eyes."; It is the chooser's sight, from which turning from the Lord could begin (Jos 24:15).; It is the chooser's own good, honoured by the king (2Sa 19:38).; It gives way to *"evil in my eyes"*, the Lord's sight (Isa 65:12).; *Why:* in Joshua and Isaiah the choice is between the Lord and other gods. With Barzillai it is a matter of where an old man, who served, will live.

19884.text: "To know between good and evil."; It is the knowing that grounds the moral choice (Isa 7:15–16).; It is the palate's knowing of pleasant and unpleasant, which fades at eighty (2Sa 19:35).; It is the weighing of words in a dispute (Job 34:3–4).; *Why:* the same knowing is turned to right and wrong, to taste, and to judgement.

19885.text: The refusing verb (H3988A).; It is refusing the evil (Isa 7:15).; It is refusing the gentle waters (Isa 8:6).; It is refusing God's terms, as Elihu charges (Job 34:33).; It is Job turning it on himself in repentance (Job 42:6).; *Why:* the act is the same; its object decides whether it is right or wrong.

19886.text: The choosing verb (H0977). It is used for choosing a master (Jos 24:15), a place (Deu 23:16), a way (Psa 119:30; Isa 66:3), a preference (Pro 16:16), and a verdict (Job 34:4). *Why:* it is turned to whatever is set before a person.

19887.text: Delight (H2654A). It is the soul's own delight in what it chose (Isa 66:3). It is the Lord's delight as the measure, either failed (Isa 65:12; 66:4) or met (Isa 56:4). *Why:* whose delight it is decides.

19888.text: Deu 23:16 and Deu 12. Whether the shared phrase is more than a shared form of words (marked "I read").

19919.text: 3.1 Deu 30:14, 17, 20, in 10.7 *Life and death set before a person*: After the Deu 30:19 sentence, add: > The passage says what choosing life is: *"loving the Lord your God, obeying his voice and holding fast to him, for he is your life and length of days"* (30:20). 19922.text: 3.4 Luk 10:42, in 10.7 *Holding a choice*, as a new bullet: > - It can be guarded by another. Mary *"sat at the Lord's feet and listened to his teaching"* (Luke 10:39).
