19923.text: 3.5 Phili 1:22–25, in 10.7 *Life and death set before a person*, as a new bullet: > - A choice between two goods can stay open. *"Yet which I shall choose I cannot tell. I am hard pressed between the two. My desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better. But to remain in the flesh is more necessary on your account"* (Philippians 1:22–24). Paul does not settle it by choosing. He goes on: *"Convinced of this, I know that I will remain and continue with you all"* (1:25).

19928.text: 3.10 Isa 66:2 beside 66:4, in 10.12 *What changes it*, *One's own conduct*: After the Isa 66:4 quote, add: > The same passage opens with the one God looks to, who *"trembles at my word"* (66:2). I read the passage as setting that trembling beside "their fears".

19929.text: 3.11 Pro 1:29, in 10.12, the *It strikes* bullet: After the Pro 1:26–27 quote, add: > The same speech says they *"did not choose the fear of the Lord"* (1:29). I read the passage as setting the fear of the Lord, not chosen, beside the terror that comes.; (Pro 1:22, *"How long, O simple ones, will you love being simple?"*, is not proposed. 10.7 *Willing* already carries the refusals of this passage.)

19932.text: Rejoicing. *"And you shall rejoice before the Lord your God in all that you undertake"* (Deu 12:18). The joy is *"before the Lord"*, and its ground is given in the same chapter: *"in which the Lord your God has blessed you"* (12:7). At the Feast of Booths the joy is the purpose of the blessing: *"because the Lord your God will bless you … so that you will be altogether joyful"* (16:15). The place is where the joy is had. The blessing is what it is about.: The joy is never had alone. Each time the household, the servants and the Levite are named in it, and at the feasts *"the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow"* too (16:11). The verse after the Feast of Weeks reminds the one rejoicing: *"You shall remember that you were a slave in Egypt"* (16:12).

19933.text: Learning to fear. The tithe is eaten at the place *"that you may learn to fear the Lord your God always"* (14:23). The fear is learned at a meal. In the same passage the money is spent *"for whatever you desire … whatever your appetite craves. And you shall eat there before the Lord your God and rejoice"* (14:26). The passage does not set the fear, the appetite and the joy against each other.

19935.text: Carefulness, against presumption. When a case is *"too difficult for you"* (17:8), the decision is sought at the place. What is asked of the person then is *"you shall be careful to do according to all that they direct you"* (17:10), and not to turn *"to the right hand or to the left"* (17:11). Presumption is the opposite, and the man who acts presumptuously dies. The end is that *"all the people shall hear and fear and not act presumptuously again"* (17:13). I read this as a person's own judgement reaching its limit and being asked to yield. The passage gives the limit (*"too difficult for you"*) and the carefulness. It does not describe the inner struggle.

19937.text: Given room away from the place. Ordinary meat need not be eaten at the chosen place. *"If the place that the Lord your God will choose to put his name there is too far from you, then you may kill … and you may eat within your towns whenever you desire"* (Deu 12:21). "Whenever you desire" is the soul's desire (*ʾawwāh*, desire, with *nepeš*, soul). It is spoken of plainly and allowed, with one limit: *"the blood is the life"* (12:23).

19938.text: Drawing a man to the place. A Levite in any town *"may come when he desires—to the place that the Lord will choose"* (18:6). The Hebrew is "with all the desire of his soul", the same words for desire and soul. He is of the tribe God chose *"to stand and minister"* (18:5), and he is given an equal share when he comes (18:8). His coming is left to that desire.

19939.text: Turned toward it from far off: For those far from the chosen city, the city is the direction of prayer. Solomon's prayer gives the hardest case, the people in captivity because they sinned: *"for there is no one who does not sin"* (1Ki 8:46). The inner turning comes in steps: *"yet if they turn their heart in the land to which they have been carried captive"* (8:47); *"and repent and plead with you … saying, 'We have sinned and have acted perversely and wickedly'"* (8:47); *"if they repent with all their heart and with all their soul in the land of their enemies … and pray to you toward their land, … the city that you have chosen"* (8:48); "Turn" and "repent" are the one verb, *šûb*. The turning happens in the enemy's land. The whole heart and the whole soul are in it. The prayer is turned toward what God chose. Solomon prays it before the one who knows hearts: *"for you, you only, know the hearts of all the children of mankind"* (8:39). He also asks God to do the turning: *"that he may incline our hearts to him"* (8:58).; Nehemiah prays from exile in the same verb. He asks God to remember his word to Moses: *"if you return to me and keep my commandments and do them, … from there I will gather them and bring them to the place that I have chosen"* (Neh 1:9). Here the return is to God himself, and the place is where he brings those who return. Nehemiah's own part comes first: he *"sat down and wept and mourned for days"* (1:4), and confessed *"Even I and my father's house have sinned"* (1:6).

19940.text: Grumbling, and seeking more. When God's choice of Aaron was challenged, Moses named what lay under it: *"would you seek the priesthood also?"* (Num 16:10). The grumbling at Aaron was against God: *"What is Aaron that you grumble against him?"* (16:11), and God calls it *"the grumblings … which they grumble against you"*, to be made to *"cease from me"* (17:5). Psalm 106 names the inner act: *"men in the camp were jealous of Moses and Aaron"* (Psa 106:16). God's reply was to make the choice plain, with the staff that sprouted. Then the grumbling became terror: *"Are we all to perish?"* (Num 17:13).

19941.text: Anger at what a choice costs. Saul to Jonathan: *"do I not know that you have chosen the son of Jesse to your own shame"* (1Sa 20:30). Saul calls the choice shame and gives his reason: *"neither you nor your kingdom shall be established"* (20:31). His anger is for his house. It goes from insult to a death sentence to a spear thrown at his own son (20:33). Jonathan's choice was made in love, *"for he loved him as he loved his own soul"* (20:17). His own anger answers his father's, and it is grief for the one he chose: *"he was grieved for David, because his father had disgraced him"* (20:34). The choice holds, sealed by an oath *"in the name of the Lord"* (20:42).

19942.text: Contempt in the heart. Michal *"saw King David leaping and dancing before the Lord, and she despised him in her heart"* (2Sa 6:16). The contempt is inward before it is spoken. When it comes out, its measure is honour before others: *"before the eyes of his servants' female servants"* (6:20). David answers by naming the choosing: *"It was before the Lord, who chose me above your father"* (6:21).

19943.text: Despising and abhorring. The servant is addressed as *"one deeply despised, abhorred by the nation"* (Isa 49:7). "Despised" is the same verb as Michal's. The verse turns it round by God's faithfulness and choosing: *"Kings shall see and arise; princes, and they shall prostrate themselves; because of the Lord, who is faithful, … who has chosen you"*.

19944.text: A conclusion drawn from ruin. *"'The Lord has rejected the two clans that he chose'? Thus they have despised my people so that they are no longer a nation in their sight"* (Jer 33:24). Others look at the state of the chosen, decide God has rejected them, and despise them on that ground. God's answer is that his choosing is as fixed as day and night (33:25–26).

19945.text: Hatred. *"If you were of the world, the world would love you as its own; but because you are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you"* (Joh 15:19). The verse gives the cause: the choosing. The world's love goes to *"its own"*. The passage says the hatred fell first on Jesus (15:18), and names under it *"because they do not know him who sent me"* (15:21).

19946.text: Rejection. *"a living stone rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen and precious"* (1Pe 2:4). The word is to reject after testing: men weighed him and set him aside.

19947.text: Whose eyes. In four of these the measure is named, and it is set against God's: *"in his own eyes"* against the place God chooses (Deu 12:8); *"before the eyes of his servants' female servants"* against *"before the Lord"* (2Sa 6:20–21); *"in their sight"* (Jer 33:24); *"rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen"* (1Pe 2:4).

19951.text: Believing in the chosen one. *"a cornerstone chosen and precious, and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame"* (1Pe 2:6). Believing brings honour. For those who do not believe, the same stone is *"a stone of stumbling"* (2:7–8).

19953.text: Knowing a choice, and arguing from it. In the dispute at Jerusalem Peter appeals to what the assembly knows: *"you know that in the early days God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe"* (Act 15:7). The purpose of God's choosing one man lies in others: that they hear and believe. Their hearts were known by God and *"cleansed … by faith"* (15:8–9). The debate ends in silence and listening (15:12), and the assembly's own choosing follows (15:25).

19954.text: Knowing that others are chosen, from what was seen. *"For we know, brothers loved by God, that he has chosen you, because our gospel came to you not only in word, but also in power and in the Holy Spirit and with full conviction"* (1Th 1:4–5). The knowing rests on what Paul saw: faith, love and hope at work (1:3), joy in affliction (1:6), and a turning *"to God from idols"* (1:9).

19955.text: Not knowing, and still used. Cyrus is called for the sake of the chosen: *"For the sake of my servant Jacob, and Israel my chosen, I call you by your name, I name you, though you do not know me"* (Isa 45:4). And *"I equip you, though you do not know me"* (45:5). Knowing is held out as the purpose: *"that you may know that it is I"* (45:3).

19956.text: Seeking, and not obtaining. *"Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened"* (Rom 11:7). The rest were seeking. They were given *"eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear"* (11:8). Paul at once refuses the conclusion that this is the end: *"did they stumble in order that they might fall? By no means!"* (11:11). The remnant is chosen *"by grace"*, not works (11:5–6). The passage says how the elect were chosen. It does not say why the rest were not.

19957.text: An inner act weighed by what God chooses: In one passage the inner act of the others is itself set against God's choosing. The people fast and ask, *"Why have we humbled ourselves, and you take no knowledge of it?"* (Isa 58:3). They *"delight to know my ways"* and *"delight to draw near to God"* (58:2). Yet *"in the day of your fast you seek your own pleasure, and oppress all your workers"* (58:3). Then: *"Is such the fast that I choose, a day for a person to humble himself?"* (58:5). "Humble himself" is the humbling of the soul, the same words as their own complaint. What God does choose is turned outward: *"to let the oppressed go free"*, *"to share your bread with the hungry"*, *"not to hide yourself from your own flesh"* (58:6–7).; The self-humbling they offered was not wrong in itself. The passage says it stood beside oppression and quarrelling in the same people, and that it was not what he chooses.

19958.text: Desire.; The soul's desire for food is given room away from the chosen place (Deu 12:21).; The soul's whole desire draws a Levite to the chosen place (Deu 18:6).; The soul delights in its own abominations, beside a wrong choice (Isa 66:3, §2a).; *Why:* what the desire is turned toward. The same words for the soul's desire are used for meat in the towns and for the Levite's coming. The verses allow both. What the soul delights in decides the third.

19959.text: Despising.; Michal despises the chosen man *"in her heart"*, by the eyes of people (2Sa 6:16, 20).; The servant is *"deeply despised"* by others, and kings will bow (Isa 49:7). Same verb, *bāzâ*.; The chosen people themselves *"despised the pleasant land"* (Psa 106:24, §2b; *māʾas*).; Others *"despised my people"*, concluding that God had rejected them (Jer 33:24; *nāʾaṣ*).; *Why:* who despises what. It is aimed at the chosen by others, and by the chosen at what they were given. Each verse names its own ground: honour before people, the chosen people's ruin, no faith in the promise.

19960.text: Fear.; It is learned at a feast in the chosen place (Deu 14:23).; It falls on those who hear of presumption punished (Deu 17:13).; It comes as terror when God makes his choice plain to grumblers: *"Are we all to perish?"* (Num 17:13).; *Why:* the setting. The first is learned in plenty, the second comes from hearing, the third from facing a choice they resisted.

19961.text: Knowing.; Knowing that God chose is ground for settling a dispute (Act 15:7).; Another's being chosen is known from what is seen (1Th 1:4–5).; Not knowing God does not stop a man from being called for the sake of the chosen (Isa 45:4–5).; Not knowing the Father is named under the world's hatred (Joh 15:21).; *Why:* whose knowing, and of what. It is the knowing of a choice, or of the God who chose.

Later they *"planned if possible to run the ship ashore"* (v39). Their looking ahead is hedged by what they cannot know.

20029.text: 10.7 Choosing and setting direction, new section *Planning* | The account of looking ahead. Planning carries a choice ahead (Gen 11:6; Pro 16:9). It covers: weighing first (Luk 14:28–33; Pro 31:15–16; Judg 19:30); planning without knowing (Act 27:10–14, 39–41; Rom 1:13; Jam 4:15); a plan carrying a person's word (2Co 1:17–18); planning together and parting (Act 15:37–39; Luk 23:51–52); planning for another's good (Dan 6:3–4), with the king's planning measured against God's (2Sa 14:13–14); a purpose held (Psa 17:3, 5; Act 11:23; 2Ti 3:10; 1Ch 29:18; Rom 8:6–7; Isa 26:3); devised from one's own heart (1Ki 12:32–33; Neh 6:8); the plan and its outcome (Pro 16:9; Isa 8:10; Act 5:38–39; Psa 21:11; Dan 11:24; Gen 50:20); seen and disclosed (1Ch 28:9; 1Co 4:3–5) | New section

20117.text: 2. The Greek: will and plan are one family: All four have the step gloss "plan". One word, G1013, is rendered "plan" in one verse and "will" in another. And G1014 is rendered "chooses": *"anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him"* (Mat 11:27; Luk 10:22). In Greek, then, willing, choosing and planning are spoken of with one family of words. This is a fact about the words. What it means for the inner being is still to be read verse by verse.; These verses join willing to planning or setting direction directly:

20140.text: Choosing (10.7) | Taking one thing over another | G1014 is rendered "chooses" (Mat 11:27)

20143.text: 5. If you want this woven: Read the 99 verses in their passages, the method used for the plan set.; Route them under rule 72. By scan, God's or the Spirit's will (route A) is 21 verses: Deu 10:10; 23:5; 29:20; Jos 24:10; 2Ki 8:19; 13:23; 24:4; 2Ch 21:7; Dan 4:17, 25, 32, 35; 5:21; Mat 11:27; Luk 10:22; Luk 22:42 (with B); Rom 9:19; 1Co 12:11; Heb 6:17; Jam 1:18; 2Pe 3:9. Job 39:9 is the wild ox (13.4 Nature).; A home in 10.7 would be a section on willing, next to *Planning* and *Holding a choice*. The working note already reserves "Will and resolve" for there.; Placed already (in the narrative for another reason, #1987): Deu 1:26; 2:30; 1Sa 31:4; Psa 51:12; Pro 6:35; Dan 5:19; Act 25:20; 1Ti 2:8. Each still needs reading for its will word.

20164.text: What the refusal goes with. In these passages the "no" to God is placed beside something the people chose or planned instead: *"But you were unwilling, and you said, 'No! We will flee upon horses'"* (Isa 30:15–16). The refusal is said in their own words, together with their own plan. The chapter opened with *"stubborn children … who carry out a plan, but not mine"* (30:1). They told the prophets, *"Do not prophesy to us what is right; speak to us smooth things"* (30:10).; *"Israel would not submit to me. So I gave them over to their stubborn hearts, to follow their own counsels"* (Psa 81:11–12).; *"Because they hated knowledge and did not choose the fear of the Lord, would have none of my counsel and despised all my reproof, therefore they shall eat the fruit of their way, and have their fill of their own devices"* (Pro 1:29–31).; *"None of them cast away the detestable things their eyes feasted on"* (Eze 20:8).; *"a hard forehead and a stubborn heart"* (Eze 3:7).

20165.text: Pro 1:29–31 and Psa 81:11–12 put choosing, willing and one's own counsels or devices into a single sentence. In Proverbs: did not choose, would have none of my counsel, their own devices. In the psalm: would not submit, their stubborn hearts, their own counsels. These are the places where Scripture itself sets the acts side by side. Both say what follows: being given over to one's own counsels, and being filled with one's own devices. They do not say these acts form one sequence in every person, and these notes do not say it either.

20202.text: The Son chooses: *"yes, Father, for such was your gracious will. All things have been handed over to me by my Father … and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him"* (Mat 11:26–27; Luk 10:21–22). The Father's gracious will and the Son's choosing stand together. Luke adds *"he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit"* (10:21).

20207.text: 2.2 Passages where Scripture itself puts them together: Pro 1:29–31. Did not choose the fear of the Lord, would have none of my counsel, are filled with their own devices: choosing, willing and devising in one sentence. Earlier in the same chapter, *"if sinners entice you, do not consent. If they say, 'Come with us, let us lie in wait for blood'"* (1:10–11) puts the will's "no" right against a group plot. That is plotting as written in 10.10.; Psa 81:11–12. Would not submit, given over to stubborn hearts, to follow their own counsels.; Isa 30:1, 9, 15–16. A plan *"but not mine"*; unwilling to hear; unwilling, and *"No! We will flee upon horses."* The refusal and the people's own plan are in their own mouth together.; 1Ch 28:19–21. The plan from the hand of the Lord, and *"every willing man who has skill"*. This is the positive pairing: a plan given, and the willing who carry it out.; Gen 24:5–8. Planning ahead allows for another person's will (*"Perhaps the woman may not be willing"*).; 2Sa 13:24–28. A planner presses another's will until it gives way, and the plan goes on to murder.; Mat 1:19–20. Unwilling, then resolved, while still considering, then redirected by God.; Act 12:3–5. Herod's intending is set beside the church's prayer.; 2Co 1:15–17. Wanting, then plans, then the question of a divided word.; Act 27:42–43. One man's wish against a group's plan.; Dan 4:27–35. Counsel offered and not taken; the human will made absolute; the Most High *"does according to his will"*; reason returned.

20228.text: Colossians 3:12: "Put on then, as God's chosen ones … compassionate hearts": The chapter begins with where the chosen now stand: *"If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above"* (v1); *"Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth"* (v2); *"your life is hidden with Christ in God"* (v3).; Then it tells them what to put away: *"Put to death therefore what is earthly in you: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry"* (v5); *"But now you must put them all away: anger, wrath, malice, slander, and obscene talk from your mouth"* (v8); They have *"put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator"* (v10).; The verse comes next: *"Put on then, as God's chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience"* (v12). "Compassionate hearts" is literally the inward parts (G4698) of compassion. The verse gives being chosen as the ground ("as God's chosen ones"), and then gives a command. The qualities are not described as already there. They are to be put on, as clothing is.; The chosen are called *"holy and beloved"*. The holiness that is the purpose of the choosing in Ephesians 1:4 is here a name the chosen already carry, and the inner qualities are still to be put on. I set the two letters side by side; neither refers to the other.; What the chosen put on is turned toward one another: *"bearing with one another and, if one has a complaint against another, forgiving each other; as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive"* (v13); *"And above all these put on love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony"* (v14); *"And let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, to which indeed you were called in one body. And be thankful"* (v15); The forgiving is measured by being forgiven. The peace is to rule in the heart.

20231.text: James 2:5: "has not God chosen those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith": The setting is an assembly that chooses where people sit: *"if you pay attention to the one who wears the fine clothing and say, 'You sit here in a good place,' while you say to the poor man, 'You stand over there'"* (v3). James names what that shows of them inside: *"have you not then made distinctions among yourselves and become judges with evil thoughts?"* (v4).; He answers their way of choosing with God's: *"Listen, my beloved brothers, has not God chosen those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom, which he has promised to those who love him?"* (v5). The poor man they sent to stand is the kind of man God chose. The assembly went by clothing. God's choice goes by something else, and its aim is that the poor be *"rich in faith"*.; The promise is to *"those who love him"*. The love here is the chosen people's love for God.; Then: *"But you have dishonored the poor man"* (v6). Choosing against God's choice is a sin: *"if you show partiality, you are committing sin"* (v9).; The faith of the chosen poor is then tested by what it does: *"What good is it, my brothers, if someone says he has faith but does not have works?"* (v14); *"So also faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead"* (v17); Abraham: *"faith was active along with his works, and faith was completed by his works … and he was called a friend of God"* (v22–23)

20235.text: The order seen in Isaiah 43:10 holds, and is widened. God chooses first, and the inner life of the chosen is the purpose: holy and blameless before him (Eph 1:4); rich in faith (Jam 2:5); saved through sanctification and belief in the truth (2Th 2:13); Ephesians puts the choosing *"before the foundation of the world"*. The one verse where people choose (Act 6:5) has the other order. The gathering chooses by what is already seen in the man.

20236.text: The chosen are told to act. Being chosen is given as the ground of commands: put on compassionate hearts, kindness, humility, meekness, patience and love (Col 3:12–14); stand firm and hold on (2Th 2:15); be diligent to confirm your calling and election, adding quality to quality (2Pe 1:5–10); This sits with batch 1: *"be strong and do it"* (1Ch 28:10).

20242.text: Ephesians 1:4 and Colossians 3:12. Holiness is the purpose of the choosing in one, and a name the chosen carry in the other. I set them side by side. Neither refers to the other.

20243.text: How God's choosing and a person's belief fit (2Th 2:13). The verse names both and does not say.

20244.text: The chapter is one long blessing of God: *"Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing"* (v3). The choosing is part of that blessing: *"even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him"* (v4).

20245.text: The love in the passage is God's: *"In love he predestined us for adoption to himself as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will"* (v4–5). The chapter goes on with what is given: *"redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses"* (v7).

20253.text: The Feast of Weeks is a feast of rejoicing: *"And you shall rejoice before the Lord your God, you and your son and your daughter, your male servant and your female servant, the Levite who is within your towns, the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow who are among you, at the place that the Lord your God will choose"* (v11). The next verse joins a remembering to it: *"You shall remember that you were a slave in Egypt; and you shall be careful to observe these statutes"* (v12). The list in v11 includes the servant and the sojourner. The verse after it reminds the one rejoicing that he was a slave.

20254.text: The Feast of Booths: *"You shall rejoice in your feast"* (v14), with the same list. Then: *"For seven days you shall keep the feast to the Lord your God at the place that the Lord will choose, because the Lord your God will bless you in all your produce and in all the work of your hands, so that you will be altogether joyful"* (v15).: "Altogether joyful" is *śāmēaḥ* (*glad*; H8056) with *ʾak* (H0389), "only" or "surely". In v15 the joy is the outcome the blessing is given for: *"will bless you … so that you will be altogether joyful"*.; The section ends: *"They shall not appear before the Lord empty-handed. Every man shall give as he is able, according to the blessing of the Lord your God that he has given you"* (v16–17).

20255.text: What these verses show of others around the choosing: At the chosen place there is a feast for remembering (Passover) and feasts for rejoicing (Weeks, Booths).; The rejoicing is commanded (v11, v14), and it is also promised as the end of the blessing (v15).; The joy takes in those with least: the servant, the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless and the widow.; Beside that joy stands the command to remember being a slave (v12).

20256.text: Deuteronomy 17:10: "And you shall be careful to do according to all that they direct you": The passage is about a case *"too difficult for you"* (v8): *"then you shall arise and go up to the place that the Lord your God will choose"*. There the priests and the judge *"shall declare to you the decision"* (v9). "Difficult" is *pālāʾ* (H6381), to be beyond one.; The person's own judgement has reached its limit, and the decision comes from the chosen place. What is asked of him then: *"you shall be careful to do according to all that they direct you"* (v10). "Careful" is *šāmar* (*to keep: careful*; H8104J).; *"You shall not turn aside from the verdict that they declare to you, either to the right hand or to the left"* (v11).; Set against carefulness is presumption: *"The man who acts presumptuously by not obeying the priest … or the judge, that man shall die"* (v12). "Presumptuously" is *zādôn* (H2087). The passage ends in those who hear of it: *"And all the people shall hear and fear and not act presumptuously again"* (v13).

20258.text: Deuteronomy 18:6: "and he may come when he desires": Two choosings stand in the passage. First the tribe: *"For the Lord your God has chosen him out of all your tribes to stand and minister in the name of the Lord, him and his sons for all time"* (v5). Then the place: a Levite living in any town *"may come when he desires—to the place that the Lord will choose, and ministers in the name of the Lord his God, like all his fellow Levites"* (v6–7).; "When he desires" is literally "with all the desire of his soul": *kol* (all; H3605) with *ʾawwāh* (desire; H0185) and *nepeš* (*soul: appetite*; H5315L). It is the same desire of the soul that is given room for meat in Deu 12:20–21. Here it is turned toward the chosen place.; The Levite has no land: *"They shall have no inheritance among their brothers; the Lord is their inheritance, as he promised them"* (v2). The law secures his share when he comes: *"then he may have equal portions to eat"* (v8).

20259.text: 1 Kings 8:48 (and 2 Chronicles 6:38): "if they repent with all their heart and with all their soul … and pray to you toward … the city that you have chosen": Solomon dedicates the house. Before the prayer he recalls two choosings: *"I chose no city out of all the tribes of Israel in which to build a house … But I chose David to be over my people Israel"* (v16). He also recalls David's heart: *"you did well that it was in your heart"* (v18). David was not allowed to build (v19).; The prayer that follows is a run of cases. In each, someone far from the house prays toward it, and Solomon asks God to hear in heaven. The heart is named throughout: *"each knowing the affliction of his own heart and stretching out his hands toward this house"* (v38); *"render to each whose heart you know, according to all his ways (for you, you only, know the hearts of all the children of mankind)"* (v39); *"that they may fear you all the days that they live in the land"* (v40); The case of v48 is the hardest one, captivity: *"If they sin against you—for there is no one who does not sin—and you are angry with them and give them to an enemy"* (v46). Then the inner turning, in steps: *"yet if they turn their heart in the land to which they have been carried captive"* (v47). Literally, "bring it back to their heart" (*šûb*, H7725N, with the heart).; *"and repent and plead with you in the land of their captors, saying, 'We have sinned and have acted perversely and wickedly'"* (v47); *"if they repent with all their heart and with all their soul in the land of their enemies … and pray to you toward their land, which you gave to their fathers, the city that you have chosen, and the house that I have built for your name"* (v48); "Repent" in v47 and v48 is *šûb* (*to return: repent*; H7725O), the same verb as "turn their heart". The turning happens in the enemy's land, far from the city. The whole heart and the whole soul are in it. The prayer is directed toward the chosen city.

20260.text: 2 Chronicles 6:38 gives the same words, with *"the land of their captivity"*. Chronicles closes the prayer differently: *"let your saints rejoice in your goodness"* (6:41).

20261.text: What these verses show of others around the choosing: The chosen city is the direction of prayer for those who are far from it, even in an enemy's land.; The inner act is a turning: first *"turn their heart"*, then repentance in words, then repentance *"with all their heart and with all their soul"*.; The prayer is made knowing *"the affliction of his own heart"* (v38), before the one who *"only"* knows the hearts (v39).; Solomon asks God to incline the heart (v58) and calls for a heart *"wholly true"* (v61). Both are asked in the same prayer.

20262.text: Nehemiah 1:9: "but if you return to me … I will gather them and bring them to the place that I have chosen": Nehemiah is in Susa when he hears of Jerusalem: *"The remnant there … is in great trouble and shame. The wall of Jerusalem is broken down"* (v3). His response is inward first: *"As soon as I heard these words I sat down and wept and mourned for days, and I continued fasting and praying before the God of heaven"* (v4).; His prayer confesses his own part: *"confessing the sins of the people of Israel, which we have sinned against you. Even I and my father's house have sinned"* (v6). Then he asks God to remember a word: *"Remember the word that you commanded your servant Moses, saying, 'If you are unfaithful, I will scatter you among the peoples, but if you return to me and keep my commandments and do them, though your outcasts are in the uttermost parts of heaven, from there I will gather them and bring them to the place that I have chosen, to make my name dwell there'"* (v8–9).; "Return" is *šûb* (H7725O), the same tag as "repent" in 1Ki 8:47–48. Here the return is *"to me"*, to God himself. The chosen place is where God brings those who return. The verse says nothing of the place before that.; The prayer ends with those who pray with him: *"your servants who delight to fear your name"* (v11). The narrative already cites this phrase in 10.9.

20264.text: At the place: rejoicing before the Lord, shared with the household, the servants, the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless and the widow (Deu 12:7, 12, 18; 16:11, 14, 15); learning to fear the Lord, at a meal where the soul's appetite is satisfied (Deu 14:23, 26); remembering, at Passover and beside the rejoicing (Deu 16:3, 12); carefulness to do what is declared there, when a matter is too hard, against presumption (Deu 17:8–13)

20265.text: Toward the place: the whole desire of a Levite's soul, which may bring him there (Deu 18:6); the turning of the heart, and repentance with all the heart and soul, prayed toward the city from an enemy's land (1Ki 8:47–48; 2Ch 6:37–38)

20266.text: Away from the place: the soul's desire for food, given room because the place is far (Deu 12:20–21)

20267.text: Back to the place: those who return to God and keep his commandments are gathered to it (Neh 1:9)

20270.text: Corrections to the HIB/qualifier file: Deu 12:21 is "away from the chosen place", not "setting" (see above).

Batch 1 read Deuteronomy 12 in full. The forms of words differ: 12:5 has *"out of all your tribes"*, 12:14 *"in one of your tribes"*, and 23:16 *"within one of your towns"*. In 23:16 the chooser is the escaped slave. The reading does not settle whether the shared phrase is more than a form of words. It stays held.

20294.text: What others do around a choice, in these verses: hate the chosen, because they are chosen out of the world (Joh 15:19); know that God chose, and settle a dispute on it (Act 15:7); believe, as the purpose of God's choosing one man (Act 15:7); seek and not obtain, and be hardened, with eyes that do not see (Rom 11:7–8); know that others are chosen, from what was seen when the gospel came (1Th 1:4–5); endure suffering for the sake of the chosen (2Ti 2:10); reject the chosen one after testing (1Pe 2:4, 7); believe in the chosen one, and not be put to shame (1Pe 2:6); love the chosen in truth (2Jo 1)

20295.text: Set against the chosen. The world's hatred (Joh 15:19) and men's rejection (1Pe 2:4) are each set against God's choosing in the same verse. Each passage says the same treatment fell first on the one who chose, or the one chosen first (Joh 15:18; 1Pe 2:4, 7).

20296.text: Whose measure. *"rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen"* (1Pe 2:4). This sits with batch 1 (Deu 12:8), batch 2 (2Sa 6:20; Jer 33:24) and §2a.

20297.text: Others knowing a choice. In Act 15:7 the assembly knows God's past choice and argues from it. In 1Th 1:4 Paul knows that the readers are chosen, from what he saw. In Joh 15:21 the haters *"do not know him who sent me"*.

20304.text: Job 15:5 — Eliphaz: "your iniquity teaches your mouth, and you choose the tongue of the crafty": Eliphaz weighs Job by his words. He opens with *"Should a wise man answer with windy knowledge"* (v2), and charges *"you are doing away with the fear of God and hindering meditation before God"* (v4). Then he names the choice: *"For your iniquity teaches your mouth, and you choose the tongue of the crafty"* (v5). He reads it this way: something inside, iniquity, teaches the mouth; the mouth then chooses a crafty tongue; From that he gives the verdict: *"Your own mouth condemns you, and not I; your own lips testify against you"* (v6).; He takes his evaluation further inside. He moves from the mouth to the heart, eyes and spirit: *"Why does your heart carry you away, and why do your eyes flash, that you turn your spirit against God and bring such words out of your mouth?"* (v12–13). For Eliphaz, the words show what the heart has chosen.; His grounds for judging are age and tradition: *"Both the gray-haired and the aged are among us, older than your father"* (v10); *"what wise men have told, without hiding it from their fathers"* (v18); His picture of the outcome is the wicked man's end (v20–35).; Set against the book's frame, his charge *"you are doing away with the fear of God"* (v4) runs against the narrator's and the Lord's *"one who feared God"* (1:1, 8). The Lord's verdict in 42:7 is on how Eliphaz spoke of God, not directly on this charge. Still, the man Eliphaz says has chosen the tongue of the crafty is the one the Lord twice calls *"my servant Job"* (42:7–8).

20307.text: Job 34:33 — Elihu: "For you must choose, and not I": Elihu frames a confession and asks whether Job will make it: *"For has anyone said to God"*: *"I have borne punishment; I will not offend any more"*; *"teach me what I do not see; if I have done iniquity, I will do it no more"* (v31–32). Then: *"Will he then make repayment to suit you, because you reject it? For you must choose, and not I; therefore declare what you know"* (v33).; Two things stand in the verse:

20308.text: The refusing word comes back. *"because you reject it"* uses H3988A, the same verb as *"refuse the evil"* in Isaiah 7:15. Elihu says Job is refusing, and that God will not repay on Job's terms because of it.

20310.text: Job 36:21 — Elihu: "this you have chosen rather than affliction": Elihu speaks *"on God’s behalf"* (v2), and his speech is about what affliction is for: *"if they are bound in chains and caught in the cords of affliction, then he declares to them their work … He opens their ears to instruction and commands that they return from iniquity"* (v8–10); *"If they listen and serve him, they complete their days in prosperity … But if they do not listen, they perish"* (v11–12); *"He delivers the afflicted by their affliction and opens their ear by adversity"* (v15); In Elihu's account, affliction is how God opens the ear.; Then he turns to Job, and what he sees in him is inward: *"you are full of the judgment on the wicked"* (v17); *"Beware lest wrath entice you into scoffing"* (v18); *"Do not long for the night"* (v20); His evaluation: *"Take care; do not turn to iniquity, for this you have chosen rather than affliction"* (v21). The choice he sees is a preference, as in Proverbs 16:16 (*"rather than"*). Of the two things before Job, affliction (H6040, the word in v15) and iniquity (H0205), Elihu says Job has taken iniquity rather than accept the affliction as the opening of his ear. The warning *"Take care"* treats the choice as still able to be turned.; He ends by pointing to God: *"who is a teacher like him?"* (v22). "Teacher" here is H4175, from the same root as *"instruct"* in Psalm 25:8, 12 (H3384).

20313.text: The refusing verb returns at the end. Elihu's *"you reject"* and Job's *"I despise … and repent"* are the same verb (34:33; 42:6), the verb of *"refuse the evil"* (Isa 7:15). In Job the choice is made when *"now my eye sees you"* (42:5). This stands beside the test reading of Jos 24, where the people chose from what they had seen.

20315.text: Where the plan stands: With batch 4, all 18 verses of §2a (less Pro 8:10) have been read, along with the three test verses. 21301.text: Call is a purposeful act of the inner being turned to God: calling or crying out to the Lord, or on his name, in need, trust, praise or worship, or refusing to.

21304.text: Call is God's own act of summoning, choosing or appointing a person or people; it bears on their inner response (faith, obedience, hope), which other words of the verse name, and is the outward act upon them.

21306.text: Call here only names, designates or labels a person, place or thing (to be called such a name, to call it so); no inner-being operation is voiced by it.

21308.text: Call is here the judgement a person puts on a thing in naming it (calling evil good, the Sabbath a delight, a fast acceptable): a valuing of the heart voiced in speech.

21311.text: Called here only names, designates or labels a person, place or thing (to be called such a name, to call it so); no inner-being operation is voiced by it.

21313.text: Called is here the outward act of summoning, addressing or sending for another person or thing; it bears on the other's response but names no inner-being operation of the one who calls.

21314.text: Called is the standing given by God's call (the vocation); it is what diligence, worthiness or walking is directed at, not an inner operation in itself.

21315.text: Called is God's own act of summoning, choosing or appointing a person or people; it bears on their inner response (faith, obedience, hope), which other words of the verse name, and is the outward act upon them.

21359.text: Offer here is the ritual or narrated presenting of an offering, a prescribed or reported act with no inner-being operation named by it.

21360.text: Offer is here the outward act of presenting a gift, proposal or favour to another person; it bears on the other's response and names no inner operation of the one who offers.

21382.text: New is here what a person's attention, desire, worship, choice or amazement is directed at (a new teaching, a new god, something new under the sun); the inner act is named by another word of the verse.

21386.text: Old here states an age, an old age or an age class (years old, an old man, young and old, the older brother); no inner-being operation is voiced by it.

21390.text: Old here dates a thing to the past (of old, the days of old, from of old) or names the people or prophets of old; no inner-being operation is voiced by it.

21408.text: Anger is here the anger, wrath, rage or fury of a person or people: a state of the heart aroused against another, a thing or God, named by the word itself.

21441.text: Consecrated here is the holiness or sacredness of a place, day, offering, oil, writing or thing set apart (a holy place, a sacred gift, the holy mountain); no inner-being operation is voiced by it.

21456.text: Holiness here is the holiness or sacredness of a place, day, offering, oil, writing or thing set apart (a holy place, a sacred gift, the holy mountain); no inner-being operation is voiced by it.

21458.text: Holy here names an attribute of God or of his rule (a righteous Lord, the scepter of uprightness, the Holy One, his holy name or Spirit, the mystery of godliness); no operation of a person's inner being is voiced by it.

21459.text: Holy here is the holiness or sacredness of a place, day, offering, oil, writing or thing set apart (a holy place, a sacred gift, the holy mountain); no inner-being operation is voiced by it.

21460.text: Holy is here the standing of those set apart for God (the holy people, the saints, a holy nation); it names what the person is brought into, not an inner operation of its own.

21470.text: Righteous is here the godly, the righteous, the upright, the wicked or the ungodly as a class of persons toward whom an act is directed or whom an event befalls (the Lord keeps the godly, do not envy the wicked, Christ died for the ungodly); the act is named by another word of the verse.

21477.text: Righteousness is here the godliness, devoutness, reverence or uprightness of a person as a state of the heart toward God or toward what is right (a devout man who feared God, godliness trained and pursued, uprightness of heart, reverence and awe).

21478.text: Righteousness is here God's own righteous, upright or holy act toward persons (judging, vindicating, saving, delivering); it is the outward act upon them and bears on their inner response, named by other words of the verse.

21503.text: Wicked is here the godly, the righteous, the upright, the wicked or the ungodly as a class of persons toward whom an act is directed or whom an event befalls (the Lord keeps the godly, do not envy the wicked, Christ died for the ungodly); the act is named by another word of the verse.

21508.text: Wickedness is here the wickedness, ungodliness or sinfulness of a person as a state or practice of the heart, set against godliness and what is right (ungodliness, a heart busy with iniquity, a wicked deed, sinful passions).
